clues.stem: Spin a 6-chamber cylinder once before pulling the trigger. Does Player 1 or Player 2 face equal 1-in-6 odds if nobody re-spins?
clues.ahaFactoid: Before anyone shoots, the single bullet sits uniformly in one of 6 slots—so conditional on reaching slot 2 it's 1/5, making unconditional odds 1/6!

clues.stem: Purists boycott casinos paying 6:5 on a two-card Blackjack because classic tables pay what richer ratio?
clues.ahaFactoid: Dropping Blackjack payouts from 3:2 ($15 on a $10 bet) to 6:5 ($12) multiplies the casino's house edge by nearly eight!

clues.stem: Why did 17th-century gambler Chevalier de Méré win betting on at least one 6 in four 1-die rolls (~51.8%)?
clues.ahaFactoid: When he lost betting on double-6 in 24 two-die rolls (49.1%), his complaint to Pascal kicked off modern probability!

clues.stem: Draw a gold coin from one of three mystery boxes (GG, GS, SS). What are the odds the OTHER coin inside that box is also gold?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because you saw a gold face, you picked one of three equally likely gold coins—and two of those three live in the GG box!

clues.stem: Trying to collect all 50 random cereal-box cards? The Coupon Collector formula says the expected boxes needed is roughly N times what?
clues.ahaFactoid: To get all 50 cards you'll average ~225 boxes—and nearly 50 of those boxes just go toward hunting the very last card!

clues.stem: Vegas Wire: Before dealing five shared cards face up on the felt, Texas Hold'em gives every player [ _____ ] hidden in their hand.
clues.ahaFactoid: Even with just two private cards, 1,326 starting pairs boil down to 169 strategic types before the Flop lands!

clues.stem: Word-Board Bulletin: Playing all seven tiles from your wooden rack in one turn earns Scrabble's famous [ _____ ] bonus!
clues.ahaFactoid: Tournament pros memorize seven-letter "bingo" stems like TISANE and RETINA just to cash in that sweet +50 bonus!

clues.stem: Monte Carlo Curio: Add up every pocket from 1 through 36 on a casino wheel and the sum famously hits [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: That spooky sum (36 x 37 / 2 = 666) earned roulette the nickname "The Devil's Game" in 19th-century salons!

clues.stem: Casino Cage Memo: On standard American gaming floors, crisp white chips equal $1, red equals $5, and green stands for [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Poker pros nickname $25 greens "quarters" and $100 black chips "hundos" or "blacks" across most U.S. cardrooms!

clues.stem: Gridiron Toss: Before kickoff, the visiting captain calls Heads or Tails as the referee spins an official [ _____ ] coin.
clues.ahaFactoid: NFL teams that call "Tails" have historically edged out "Heads" slightly in Super Bowl coin tosses!

clues.stem: Cosmic Shuffler: With 52! ways to order one deck (an 8 followed by 67 zeroes), every real shuffle creates a [ _____ ] layout.
clues.ahaFactoid: There are more ways to stack 52 cards than atoms on Earth—so odds are your freshly shuffled deck is unique in history!

clues.stem: Sportsbook Slate: Seeing "-200" beside a heavy favorite means you must risk [ _____ ] just to win $100 in profit.
clues.ahaFactoid: Meanwhile "+200" on an underdog flips the math: a $100 ticket cashes out $200 in pure profit if the upset hits!

clues.stem: Coincidence Debunker: Diaconis and Mosteller noted that with a huge sample size, any outrageous quirk becomes [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Even a one-in-a-million fluke happens around 330 times a day in a nation of 330 million people!

clues.stem: Hospital Stats Shock: Treatment A can beat Treatment B in mild AND severe wards separately, yet lose overall via [ _____ ]!
clues.ahaFactoid: Known as Simpson's Paradox, weighted group sizes flip the combined percentage when one group draws tougher cases!

clues.stem: Measure Theory Bulletin: If the sum of event probabilities stays finite, the Borel-Cantelli lemma says infinitely many hits occur with [ _____ ] odds.
clues.ahaFactoid: Finite total probability means the tail fades fast enough that you are almost surely done hitting rare surprises!

clues.stem: Picture four Aces fanned across green felt: two shine bright red Hearts and Diamonds, while the two black Aces show Clubs and what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Early 15th-century Italian decks used swords, cups, coins, and batons before French printers turned swords into Spades!

clues.stem: Inspect the King of Hearts closely on most Bicycle decks: unlike his moustache-free cousin of Clubs, why is he nicknamed the "Suicide King"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Woodblock printers accidentally wore down the King's axe blade into a weird sword-into-head silhouette centuries ago!

clues.stem: Spot the iconic twenty-sided jewel of tabletop dungeons: rolling a natural 20 scores a critical hit, while rolling a 1 triggers what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Each face of a fair d20 carries an exact 5% chance—making dramatic fumbles just as frequent as heroic nat-20s!

clues.stem: On the Monitor: Two glowing colored circles overlap in the middle to show items belonging to BOTH sets at once. Who invented this chart?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cambridge logician John Venn introduced his overlapping circles in 1880—originally calling them "Eulerian circles"!

clues.stem: Snap! Press down on the clear plastic dome in the center of the board and a trapped six-sided die pops inside! Which 1965 classic features this bubble?
clues.ahaFactoid: Kohner Brothers invented the Pop-O-Matic dome in 1965 to keep kids from losing dice—or cheating with sneaky wrist rolls!

clues.stem: Peek at the four Jacks in a standard deck: two look straight out with both eyes, while which two Jacks stand in side profile?
clues.ahaFactoid: That's why poker "one-eyed Jacks wild" names the Jacks of Spades and Hearts—alongside the profile King of Diamonds!

clues.stem: On the Monitor: A six-pointed wooden star holds colorful marbles racing into the opposite triangle. Where was "Chinese Checkers" invented?
clues.ahaFactoid: Called "Sternhalma" in 1892 Germany, U.S. marketers slapped "Chinese Checkers" on the box in 1928 for exotic flair!

clues.stem: Look at Francis Anscombe's four famous scatter plots: a straight line, a smooth curve, a line with one outlier—all share the exact same what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Anscombe crafted those four datasets in 1973 to prove you must ALWAYS graph your data instead of trusting summary stats!

clues.stem: On the Monitor: A diamond-shaped honeycomb of hexagons where White connects left-to-right and Black top-to-bottom can NEVER end in a what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Invented independently by Piet Hein and John Nash in the 1940s, Hex's impossibility of a draw is equivalent to Brouwer's fixed-point theorem!

clues.stem: Picture parallel floorboards spaced width D apart while you drop pins of length D at random. The crossing rate lets you estimate what constant?
clues.ahaFactoid: Count N drops and C line crossings in Buffon's needle drop, and 2N/C estimates Pi—one of history's earliest Monte Carlo tricks!

clues.stem: Casino Klaxon! Three of these card-and-coin facts hold water, while one stubborn streak superstition fools gamblers nightly. Nab the myth!
clues.ahaFactoid: A fair coin has no calendar or memory—even after ten straight Tails, the next flip stays strictly 50/50!

clues.stem: Game-Night Klaxon! Three of these Monopoly rules appear in Parker Brothers' official rulebook, while one beloved house rule is FAKE!
choices: Banks can run out of houses
clues.ahaFactoid: Official Monopoly rules give ZERO cash on Free Parking—that tax pot is why home games drag on for four hours!

clues.stem: Family Table Klaxon! Three of these Uno facts are official Mattel rules, while one chaotic dorm-room habit breaks the printed rulebook!
choices: Say Uno on your last card
clues.ahaFactoid: Mattel tweeted publicly to break hearts: you CANNOT stack Draw-2 or Draw-4 cards in official Uno rules!

clues.stem: Lotto Desk Klaxon! Three of these lottery facts are pure math truth, while one popular ticket-picking tip is pure superstition!
clues.ahaFactoid: Every ball mix has identical odds every drawing—though avoiding 1-2-3-4-5-6 keeps you from splitting the pot with thousands of folks!

clues.stem: Table Klaxon! Three of these Blackjack rules are true in casinos, while one angry myth blames tablemates for "taking your bust card"!
clues.ahaFactoid: A stranger's sloppy hit is equally likely to hand the dealer a bust card or a 20—your long-run expected odds barely budge!

clues.stem: Betting Klaxon! Three of these facts about doubling after losses (the Martingale system) are true, while one pitch is a bankrupting lie!
clues.ahaFactoid: Ten straight losses turn a $5 bet into $5,120—smashing casino table limits and wiping out weeks of tiny $5 wins in one cold streak!

clues.stem: Showdown Klaxon! Three of these poker rankings are gospel in Texas Hold'em, while one playground rumor invents fake suit ranks!
choices: Four of a Kind beats Full
clues.ahaFactoid: In standard poker, ALL four suits carry identical rank—two players holding matching Royal Flushes simply split the pot!

clues.stem: Math Klaxon! Three statements describe the true Law of Large Numbers, while one twists it into the bogus "Law of Averages"!
clues.ahaFactoid: Future coins don't pay off past debt! The fraction of Heads approaches 50% simply because early streaks get diluted by millions of flips!

clues.stem: Lab Stats Klaxon! Three facts about statistical p-values are strictly right, while one textbook blunder trips up even published scientists!
clues.ahaFactoid: A p-value of 0.04 does NOT mean a 4% chance the null hypothesis is true—it measures how surprising the data are IF the null were true!

clues.stem: Game Theory Klaxon! Three truths hold for Nash Equilibria in finite games, while one wishful claim fails spectacularly in the Prisoner's Dilemma!
clues.ahaFactoid: Mutual betrayal is a Nash Equilibrium even when both players get worse payoffs—why traffic jams and arms races trap rational actors!

clues.stem: 50/50 Chess Rule: At the opening gong of a standard Chess match, which side ALWAYS makes the very first move?
clues.ahaFactoid: Modern rules locked White's first-move tradition around 1880—giving White a slight ~54% historical edge in grandmaster play!

clues.stem: 50/50 Dice Bet: Roll two standard 6-sided dice and add them up. Is the sum MORE likely to be even, odd, or dead tied?
clues.ahaFactoid: Wait—6 ways to get 7 (odd) balance out 2+4+6+8+10+12 (even): 18 even sums and 18 odd sums make it a pure 50/50!

clues.stem: Game-Show Showdown: After picking Door #1 and watching the host reveal a goat behind Door #3, should you switch to Door #2 or stay?
clues.ahaFactoid: Your original pick keeps its 1-in-3 shot, while the remaining closed door inherits the whole 2-in-3 pool!

clues.stem: 50/50 Tile Bag: Inside a standard English Scrabble set, how many E tiles sit in the bag (more than any other letter)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Twelve E tiles make E the undisputed king of the Scrabble bag, ahead of A and I with nine apiece!

clues.stem: Deck Math Showdown: Drawing cards WITHOUT putting them back makes consecutive pulls independent or dependent events?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because each removed card shrinks the remaining pool from 52 to 51, what you drew first reshapes the next card's odds!

clues.stem: 50/50 Data Call: When one billionaire walks into a neighborhood diner, which stat shoots WAY higher while the other stays calm?
clues.ahaFactoid: One extreme outlier drags the arithmetic Mean sky-high, which is why economists track Median household income instead!

clues.stem: Medical Test Paradox: A 99%-accurate test screens a 1-in-1,000 disease. If you test positive, is your chance of actually having it above or below 50%?
clues.ahaFactoid: Out of 1,000 people, 1 sick person tests positive while ~10 healthy folks trigger false alarms—so 1 in 11 positives is truly sick!

clues.stem: Coin-Doubling Bet: Pay $2 for Heads on flip 1, $4 on flip 2, $8 on flip 3 forever. Is the theoretical expected payout finite or infinite?
clues.ahaFactoid: Each step contributes $1 (1/2 x 2 + 1/4 x 4 + 1/8 x 8), summing to infinity—yet Daniel Bernoulli noted few folks pay $25 to play!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on the U.S. Map: Which American state covers MORE total square miles of territory?
clues.ahaFactoid: At 665,384 square miles, Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas—and larger than Texas, California, and Montana combined!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on the World Globe: Which of these oceans holds MORE total water surface area?
clues.ahaFactoid: Covering roughly 27.2 million square miles, the Indian Ocean ranks third globally—nearly five times bigger than the Arctic!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in New England: Which U.S. state covers FEWER total square miles than every other state?
clues.ahaFactoid: Nicknamed Little Rhody, Rhode Island spans just 1,545 square miles—small enough to fit inside Alaska more than 425 times!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Iconic Landmarks: Which famous monument stands TALLER from ground base to tip?
clues.ahaFactoid: Topping out at 1,083 feet with its broadcast spire, Paris's iron lattice tower rises nearly double the 630-foot Gateway Arch!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower by Continent: Which continent contains MORE independent UN-recognized countries?
clues.ahaFactoid: Home to 54 sovereign nations from Algeria to Zimbabwe, Africa holds more countries than any other continent on Earth!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in U.S. Latitude: Which U.S. state reaches FARTHER SOUTH toward the Equator?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ka Lae (South Point) on Hawaii's Big Island reaches 18.9°N—nearly 400 miles closer to the Equator than Key West!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on U.S. Rivers: Which mighty North American waterway flows MORE total miles?
clues.ahaFactoid: Stretching 2,341 miles from Montana's Rockies to St. Louis, the Missouri edges out the Mississippi by roughly 100 miles!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on Summit Charts: Which mountain chain reaches HIGHER peak elevation above sea level?
clues.ahaFactoid: The Himalayas pack all 14 of Earth's 8,000-meter peaks, whereas the Andes top out at Argentina's 22,837-foot Aconcagua!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in City Crowds: Which metropolitan area packs MORE total residents?
clues.ahaFactoid: Roughly 37 million people live across Greater Tokyo—nearly double the population of the entire New York metro region!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Time Zones: Which sunny hub greets the new calendar morning EARLIER?
clues.ahaFactoid: Sitting at UTC+12 (and +13 in summer), Auckland sees sunrise three hours ahead of Tokyo and twelve hours before London!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Latitude: Which national capital sits FARTHER NORTH toward the Arctic Circle?
clues.ahaFactoid: Iceland's geothermal capital sits just two degrees shy of the Arctic Circle, beating Helsinki, Oslo, and Stockholm!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on Shorelines: Which U.S. state boasts MORE miles of jagged tidal coastline?
clues.ahaFactoid: Counting islands and fjords, Alaska's 33,904 miles of tidal shoreline exceed every other U.S. state combined!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Great Lakes Depth: After Lake Superior, which Great Lake plunges DEEPER beneath its surface?
clues.ahaFactoid: Shallow Lake Erie averages just 62 feet deep, whereas Lake Michigan drops more than 920 feet down to cold bedrock!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in U.S. Altitude: Which state averages the HIGHEST mean elevation above sea level?
clues.ahaFactoid: Even Colorado's very LOWEST point on the Arikaree River sits 3,317 feet up—higher than the highest hill in 18 states!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Time Zones: Counting overseas departments and islands, which country spans MORE time zones?
clues.ahaFactoid: From French Polynesia to Reunion to Guiana, France spans 12 time zones (13 in summer)—beating Russia's 11 contiguous zones!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on Latitude Lines: Which famous city actually sits FARTHER NORTH on the globe?
clues.ahaFactoid: Mild Mediterranean air fools travelers—gondola-filled Venice sits at 45.4°N, well north of New York City (40.7°N) and even Toronto!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Canadian Lakes: Which lake lying WHOLLY inside Canada covers MORE square miles?
clues.ahaFactoid: Spanning 12,028 square miles straddling the Arctic Circle, Great Bear Lake is the largest lake entirely inside Canada!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Neighbors: Counting sovereign land borders only, which nation touches MORE countries?
clues.ahaFactoid: Both China and Russia share land borders with 14 sovereign nations—the highest total on the world map!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in South American Capitals: Which capital city sits at a HIGHER altitude above sea level?
clues.ahaFactoid: Perched on a lush Andean plateau, Bogota ranks as the third-highest capital in South America behind La Paz and Quito!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in the European Alps: Which famous snowy summit stands HIGHER above sea level?
clues.ahaFactoid: Rising on the French-Italian border, Mont Blanc rules Western Europe—connected underneath by a 7.2-mile highway tunnel!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Rainfall: Which bizarre polar or desert spot averages LESS yearly precipitation?
clues.ahaFactoid: Fierce 200-mph katabatic winds evaporate snow before it lands, leaving parts of Antarctica's Dry Valleys rainless for roughly 2 million years!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Western Europe: Which famous river flows MORE total miles from Alpine headwaters to the sea?
clues.ahaFactoid: Winding 760 miles through Switzerland, Germany, and the Netherlands, the Rhine carries more commercial barges than the Loire or Seine!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in North America: Three of these are official Great Lakes, while one belongs to Utah!
clues.ahaFactoid: Remember HOMES (Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior)—Utah's salty basin is a remnant of prehistoric Lake Bonneville!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on the Border: Three of these U.S. states touch Mexico directly, while one sits one state north!
clues.ahaFactoid: California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas form the U.S.-Mexico border—while Nevada stops at Arizona and California!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on the Flagpole: Three countries fly red, white, and blue flags, while one flies bright GREEN instead!
clues.ahaFactoid: Ireland's green-white-orange tricolor symbolizes Catholic green, Protestant orange, and peace in white between them!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Africa: Three of these nations sit on the African continent, while one sits on the Arabian Peninsula!
clues.ahaFactoid: Separated from Djibouti by the narrow Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, Yemen anchors the southwestern corner of Asia!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in New York City: Three of these are official NYC boroughs, while one is a separate state across the Hudson!
clues.ahaFactoid: New York's five boroughs are Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, The Bronx, and Staten Island—while Frank Sinatra's Hoboken sits in New Jersey!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Polynesia: Three of these are major Hawaiian islands, while one sits way down in the Caribbean!
clues.ahaFactoid: Part of the sunny Dutch ABC islands off Venezuela, Aruba sits thousands of miles east of Hawaii's volcanic chain!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Europe: Three of these famous landmarks stand in London, while one stands proudly in Rome!
clues.ahaFactoid: Tossing a coin over your left shoulder into Rome's baroque Trevi Fountain supposedly guarantees a return trip to Italy!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in U.S. Postal Codes: Three of these states begin with the word "New," while one is a Canadian province!
clues.ahaFactoid: The four "New" U.S. states are New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, and New York—New Brunswick sits on Canada's Bay of Fundy!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Capitals: Three of these famous cities serve as their country's official capital, while one does NOT!
clues.ahaFactoid: Sydney is Australia's biggest city, yet Canberra won the 1908 compromise to become the nation's official capital!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Northern Europe: Three of these Nordic nations touch the Scandinavian region, while one is Alpine!
clues.ahaFactoid: Sitting deep in Central Europe's Alps along the Danube, Vienna's Austria lies far south of Viking Scandinavia!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on the Water: Three of these are completely surrounded by ocean as islands, while one is a peninsula!
clues.ahaFactoid: Surrounded on three sides by the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico, Florida stays firmly attached to Georgia and Alabama!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in South America: Three of these nations use Spanish as their official language, while one uses English!
clues.ahaFactoid: Formerly British Guiana, coastal Guyana is the only sovereign South American country where English is the official language!

clues.stem: Odd One Out at Four Corners: Three of these states meet at America's famous quadripoint monument, while one misses out!
clues.ahaFactoid: Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico touch at one granite brass marker—the only point where four U.S. states meet!

clues.stem: Odd One Out Along the Danube: Three of these European capitals sit directly on the Danube River, while one sits on the Vistula!
clues.ahaFactoid: The Danube links Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade—while Poland's Warsaw sits proudly on the Vistula!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on the Coast: Three of these Alpine/Central nations are landlocked with zero sea coast, while one touches the Adriatic!
clues.ahaFactoid: Though its coastline spans barely 29 miles around medieval Piran and Koper, Slovenia opens straight onto the Adriatic Sea!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on Island Hopping: Three of these sit inside the Mediterranean Sea, while one lies out in the Atlantic!
clues.ahaFactoid: Portuguese Madeira perches off Morocco in the open North Atlantic—famous for fortified wine and Cristiano Ronaldo's birthplace!

clues.stem: Odd One Out at 0° Latitude: Three of these nations are sliced straight across by the Equator, while one sits entirely north!
clues.ahaFactoid: Not a single inch of Mexico crosses the Equator—even its southern Chiapas border stops around 14.5° North!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Statehouses: Three of these cities are state capitals that are NOT their state's biggest city, while one IS both!
clues.ahaFactoid: Boston towers as Massachusetts' capital AND largest hub—while Los Angeles, NYC, and Houston outsize their capitals!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Northern Flags: Three of these northern nations fly the classic Nordic cross, while one flies horizontal stripes!
clues.ahaFactoid: Estonia's crisp blue-black-white tricolor mirrors sky, soil, and winter snow—though some Estonians occasionally debate adopting a Nordic cross!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on Charts: Three of these waterways connect naturally to the world's oceans, while one is an inland freshwater lake!
clues.ahaFactoid: Despite its grand title, the Sea of Galilee (Lake Kinneret) is Earth's lowest freshwater lake at roughly 700 feet below sea level!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Transcontinental Hubs: Three of these countries span two continents, while one sits wholly inside Asia!
clues.ahaFactoid: Kazakhstan's far western tip crosses the Ural River into Europe, whereas landlocked Mongolia sits 100% inside Asia!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on 0° Longitude: Three of these nations cross the Prime Meridian line, while one lies completely WEST of it!
clues.ahaFactoid: The 0° Greenwich line slices through Britain, France, Spain, Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo, and Ghana—well east of Dakar, Senegal!

clues.stem: 1977 Bumper-Sticker Icon: Milton Glaser drew a chunky black letter, a bright red heart, and two stacked letters to spell [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Glaser scribbled the legendary logo on a torn envelope in the back of a yellow cab—and drew it completely for free to cheer NYC up!

clues.stem: 2003 Tourism Smash: Neon billboards promised wild freedom with the wink, "What happens here, [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Ad agency R&R Partners launched the line in 2003—making Las Vegas's slogan one of the most parodied lines in travel history!

clues.stem: 1969 Welcome Sign: Originally pitched for history and beach fans alike, Virginia's timeless travel slogan reads, "Virginia is for [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Copywriter Robin McLaughlin's three-word hook debuted in Modern Bride magazine in 1969 and never left highway welcome signs!

clues.stem: 1986 Anti-Litter Campaign: Highway signs told pickup drivers not to toss beer cans with the swaggering warning, "Don't [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Featuring Stevie Ray Vaughan and Willie Nelson, the slogan slashed Texas roadside litter by roughly 72% in its first four years!

clues.stem: 24/7 Subway Energy: Frank Sinatra crooned about waking up in Manhattan, famous worldwide as "the city that [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Fort Wayne, Indiana actually used "The City That Never Sleeps" in a 1912 newspaper ad before New York claimed the crown!

clues.stem: Big Easy Toast: Celebrating Louisiana's French-Creole spirit, New Orleans revelers live by "Laissez les bons [ _____ ]" (Let the good times roll).
clues.ahaFactoid: Though French-speaking Cajuns and Creoles popularized it in Louisiana, the phrase actually originated in English first and got translated back!

clues.stem: Granite State Plate: Emblazoned across New Hampshire license plates since 1971, General John Stark's 1809 toast vows, "Live Free or [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Ironically, New Hampshire state prison inmates stamped "Live Free or Die" onto metal license plates for decades!

clues.stem: Travel Etiquette Advice: St. Ambrose told St. Augustine to follow local customs wherever you visit—inspiring "When in Rome, do as the [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: In 387 CE, Ambrose simply meant fasting on Saturdays in Rome and feasting in Milan—no sightseeing required!

clues.stem: 1849 Rush Nickname: Celebrating both poppy fields and Sutter's Mill nuggets, California appears on maps as the [ _____ ] State.
clues.ahaFactoid: California shares its golden theme with the Golden Gate Strait—named in 1846 BEFORE gold was even spotted in 1848!

clues.stem: Local Indie Motto: Printed on thousands of T-shirts and coffee mugs, Texas's capital rallies behind the bumper sticker "Keep [ _____ ] Weird."
clues.ahaFactoid: Librarian Red Wassenich coined the phrase calling in to an Austin radio pledge drive in 2000—later imitated by Portland!

clues.stem: Orange-Grove Plates: Stamped across millions of white-and-orange license plates since 1949, Florida proudly bills itself as the [ _____ ] State.
clues.ahaFactoid: Before settling on Sunshine State in 1949, Florida briefly touted itself as the "Everglade State" and "Peninsula State"!

clues.stem: Northern Anthem Line: Canadians belt out "O Canada" saluting their vast homeland as "The [ _____ ] strong and free!"
clues.ahaFactoid: The lyrics also salute a land stretching "from sea to sea"—though Canada actually touches THREE oceans (Atlantic, Pacific, Arctic)!

clues.stem: 1865 Frontier Call: Newspaper editor Horace Greeley popularized the pioneer push often quoted as "Go [ _____ ], young man!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Greeley likely echoed Terre Haute editor John Soule—encouraging job-seekers to seek farmland across the prairies!

clues.stem: Airport Farewell: Humphrey Bogart comforts Ingrid Bergman on a misty Casablanca runway with the line, "We'll always have [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Despite its Moroccan setting, Casablanca was filmed entirely on Warner Bros. backlots in Burbank, California!

clues.stem: Skeptical Motto: Rep. Willard Vandiver told an 1899 crowd he came from a state that raises corn and cotton—giving Missouri the tag "The [ _____ ] State."
clues.ahaFactoid: Vandiver famously added, "Frothy eloquence neither convinces nor satisfies me. I am from Missouri. You have got to show me."

clues.stem: 18th-Century Grand Tour: Goethe marveled at Mount Vesuvius and a sparkling Italian bay, quoting the old proverb "See [ _____ ] and die."
clues.ahaFactoid: Italian "Vedi Napoli e poi muori" simply meant no sight on Earth could top the Bay of Naples afterward!

clues.stem: Renaissance Cartography: While medieval mapmakers painted sea monsters on uncharted seas, the Hunt-Lenox Globe bears the Latin warning "Here be [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Engraved around 1510 on a grapefruit-sized copper globe in New York's Public Library, "Hic sunt dracones" is one of very few real examples!

clues.stem: Becalmed in the Doldrums: Coleridge's stranded sailor groans beside salty ocean swells, "Water, water, everywhere, nor any drop to [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Early sailing ships drifting across the windless Horse Latitudes and Doldrums often ran dangerously low on fresh drinking water!

clues.stem: Global Meridian Reach: First coined for 16th-century Spain before fitting Queen Victoria's globe-spanning realm, "the empire on which the [ _____ ] never sets."
clues.ahaFactoid: Because of tiny Pitcairn Island in the Pacific, the sun technically STILL never sets on all British Overseas Territories at once!

clues.stem: Maori Archipelago Name: Translating "Aotearoa," explorers christened New Zealand "The Land of the Long White [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Polynesian navigators spotted long cumulus ribbons lingering over snow-capped peaks days before the green islands rose into view!

clues.stem: 1844 Oregon Border Rally: U.S. expansionists demanded the northern Pacific boundary up to Russian Alaska with the cry, "[ _____ ] or Fight!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Instead of fighting Britain, President James K. Polk settled peacefully on the 49th parallel—giving Washington and Oregon to the U.S.!

clues.stem: Pillars of Hercules Flip: After 1492 voyages proved oceans didn't end at Gibraltar, Spain adopted the royal motto "Plus [ _____ ]" (Further Beyond).
clues.ahaFactoid: Ancient myth warned sailors "Non Plus Ultra" (Nothing Further Beyond) at Gibraltar—until Atlantic crossings inspired Spain's two-pillar banner!

clues.stem: I sit cold in San Francisco Bay, once locked up Al Capone behind iron bars, and got named after pelicans by Spanish sailors. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: La Isla de los Alcatraces meant "Island of the Gannets" (pelicans)—long before it became America's most famous maximum-security prison!

clues.stem: I plug Black Canyon between Nevada and Arizona with 4.36 million cubic yards of concrete, forming massive Lake Mead. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Finished two years ahead of schedule in 1936, its thick concrete base is 660 feet wide—as deep as two football fields end to end!

clues.stem: I sprawl beside the Nile Delta as Africa's largest metro, gazing straight across the river toward Giza's ancient pyramids. What city am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Founded by the Fatimids in 969 CE as Al-Qahirah ("The Victorious"), Cairo hosts more than 20 million bustling residents today!

clues.stem: Sculptor Gutzon Borglum blasted 450,000 tons of South Dakota granite to carve four 60-foot presidential faces into my cliff. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Behind Abraham Lincoln's forehead sits an unfinished secret granite Hall of Records sealing porcelain plaques of U.S. history!

clues.stem: I stretch beside the Kremlin's brick towers and onion domes of St. Basil's Cathedral—my Russian name originally meant "beautiful." What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Russian "krasnaya" once meant both "beautiful" and "red"—meaning Red Square earned its name centuries before the Soviet flag!

clues.stem: My Latin name means "in the middle of the land"—I link Gibraltar to Suez while washing beaches from Spain to Greece. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Roughly 5.3 million years ago, a broken Gibraltar dam refilled the dried Mediterranean basin in the cataclysmic Zanclean flood!

clues.stem: Jazz trumpets echo through my French Quarter, below-sea-level levees curve like a crescent moon, and Mardi Gras parades roll. What city am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because French Quarter streets hug a natural Mississippi bend, locals don't say north or south—they navigate "lakeside" and "riverside"!

clues.stem: Opened in 1883 across the East River, I proved my steel cables could hold weight by marching 21 circus elephants across my deck! What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Showman P.T. Barnum paraded Jumbo and 20 fellow elephants across the bridge in May 1884 to calm nervous New Yorkers!

clues.stem: I became a crisp red-white-red national banner on February 15, 1965, putting an eleven-pointed autumn leaf center stage. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Wind-tunnel tests proved a bold 11-point silhouette stayed readable at a distance way better than a complex 13-point botanical leaf!

clues.stem: I rose 102 stories in just 410 days during the Depression, hosted King Kong on my mast, and ruled NYC's skyline for 40 years. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Architects topped it with a shiny dirigible mooring mast—though wild Midtown crosswinds made docking blimps way too dangerous!

clues.stem: Look at my shape on a U.S. map and you'll spot a mitten plus an Upper Peninsula—connected by the five-mile Mackinac Bridge. What state am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Residents in Michigan's Upper Peninsula call themselves "Yoopers" and fondly nickname Lower Peninsula folks "Trolls" (under the bridge)!

clues.stem: I am the only national capital on Earth with a wild lion-and-giraffe national park sitting right along my airport skyline! What city am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Minutes from downtown skyscrapers, Nairobi National Park lets commuters spot rhinos and giraffes grazing against office towers!

clues.stem: I span California and Nevada, shelter spiky Joshua trees, and cradle scorching Death Valley inside my borders. What desert am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Smallest of North America's four major deserts, the Mojave draws a crisp botanical boundary wherever twisted Joshua trees grow!

clues.stem: I circle the globe near 23.4° North, marking the northernmost line where the June solstice noon sun shines straight overhead. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Named 2,000 years ago when the June sun stood in the constellation Cancer—though axial wobble has shifted it into Taurus today!

clues.stem: Covering most of Botswana, my red sand basin hosts desert elephants, meerkats, and seasonal wetlands in the Okavango. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because parts of the Kalahari get up to 20 inches of summer rain, geographers call much of it a semi-arid savanna rather than true sand waste!

clues.stem: On Spain's Mediterranean coast, my sunlit avenues weave Antoni Gaudi's melted stone curves toward a still-rising cathedral. What city am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Barcelona's Eixample grid features chamfered octagonal street corners engineered in 1859 so horse trams could turn smoothly!

clues.stem: I rise 14,411 feet as Washington State's icy volcanic crown, towering above Puget Sound on crisp Seattle mornings. What peak am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Capped by 25 major glaciers—more than any other mountain in the Lower 48—Rainier also ranks as a closely watched active volcano!

clues.stem: Hugging southeast Africa along the Indian Ocean across from Madagascar, my green-yellow-black flag famously depicts a book, hoe, and rifle. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Mozambique's 1983 flag pairs a rifle for defense, a hoe for farming, and an open book for education—unique among national flags!

clues.stem: Carving the border past Montreal and Quebec City, I carry ocean freighters all the way from the Atlantic into the Great Lakes. What river am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Opened in 1959, the St. Lawrence Seaway locks lift massive cargo ships 600 feet above sea level into Lake Superior!

clues.stem: I wind 350 treacherous miles between mainland South America and Tierra del Fuego, sparing early ships from rounding stormy Cape Horn. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Magellan needed 38 foggy days in 1520 to thread its twisting narrows—naming the southern shore "Land of Fire" from indigenous bonfires!

clues.stem: Sitting 92 feet BELOW global sea level along the oil-rich Caspian shore, I hold the title of Earth's lowest-lying national capital. What city am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Azerbaijan's windy capital blends medieval stone Maiden Tower walls with futuristic flame-shaped skyscrapers!

clues.stem: Cradled between the Tian Shan and Kunlun mountains in China's Tarim Basin, my shifting dunes carry a name folk-glossed as "go in, never come out." What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ancient Silk Road caravans hugged the Taklamakan's northern and southern oases rather than risking a direct crossing!

clues.stem: Before or After in Landmarks: Which world-famous iron or steel monument opened to visitors FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Gustave Eiffel unveiled his Paris tower for the 1889 World's Fair—nearly 50 years before San Francisco's Golden Gate opened in 1937!

clues.stem: Before or After in Engineering: Which monumental ship-or-barge canal opened to traffic FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Linked across 1,100 miles by the Sui Dynasty in the 600s CE, China's Grand Canal predates Suez (1869) by over twelve centuries!

clues.stem: Before or After in U.S. Statehood: Which 20th-century newcomer joined the United States LAST (as the 50th state)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hawaii entered the Union on August 21, 1959—seven months after Alaska joined in January 1959!

clues.stem: Before or After in Famous Bridges: Which iconic river span opened to commuters FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: London's bascule-lifting Tower Bridge opened in 1894—43 years before San Francisco's Golden Gate opened in 1937!

clues.stem: Before or After in Travel Parks: Which Disney resort welcomed families FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Walt Disney opened Anaheim's Disneyland in July 1955—16 years before Orlando's Magic Kingdom debuted in October 1971!

clues.stem: Before or After in National Parks: Which scenic treasure became the world's FIRST official National Park?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ulysses S. Grant signed Yellowstone into law in 1872—creating the world's first national park before Wyoming was even a state!

clues.stem: Before or After on Road Trips: Which famous U.S. highway milestone arrived FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Commissioned in November 1926 from Chicago to Santa Monica, Route 66 predated the 1956 Interstate Highway Act by 30 years!

clues.stem: Before or After Underground: Which world city opened its first subterranean passenger subway train FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: London's steam-powered Metropolitan Railway opened in 1863—more than 40 years before New York City's subway debuted in 1904!

clues.stem: Before or After in Exploration: Which extreme Earth prize did human explorers reach FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Roald Amundsen planted Norway's flag at the South Pole in December 1911—42 years before Hillary and Norgay topped Everest!

clues.stem: Before or After in Skylines: Which soaring tower claimed the title of world's tallest structure MOST RECENTLY?
clues.ahaFactoid: Opening in January 2010 at 2,717 feet, Burj Khalifa shattered records once held by Empire State (1931), Sears/Willis (1973), and CN Tower (1975)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Planned Capitals: Which purpose-built national capital was officially inaugurated FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: U.S. Congress moved into Washington, D.C. in 1800—well ahead of Canberra (1927), Brasilia (1960), and Islamabad (1960s)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Young Nations: Among these post-1990 independent countries, which joined the UN as an independent state FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Eritrea gained independence in 1993—ahead of Timor-Leste (2002), Montenegro (2006), and South Sudan (2011)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Undersea Tunnels: Which engineering marvel opened to trains FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Japan's Seikan rail tunnel linking Honshu and Hokkaido opened in 1988—six years before the Eurostar Chunnel opened in 1994!

clues.stem: Before or After on U.S. Maps: Which territory entered the United States as an official state FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Louisiana joined the Union in 1812—well ahead of Texas (1845), California (1850), and Oregon (1859)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Indian Cities: Which famous colonial-era city name switched FIRST in the 1990s-2000s?
clues.ahaFactoid: Maharashtra renamed Bombay to Mumbai in 1995—followed by Madras becoming Chennai (1996) and Calcutta becoming Kolkata (2001)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Timekeeping: When did international delegates vote Greenwich, London as the 0° Prime Meridian?
clues.ahaFactoid: France actually abstained at the 1884 conference and kept clinging to "Paris Mean Time" on maps until 1911!

clues.stem: Before or After in Atlas Changes: Which peaceful European border shift occurred FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: East and West Germany reunited on October 3, 1990—ahead of the 1993 Velvet Divorce and 1995 Schengen launch!

clues.stem: Before or After in U.S. Expansion: Which territorial milestone happened FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Jefferson doubled the U.S. in 1803, Seward bought Alaska in 1867, Hawaii joined in 1898, and Denmark sold the Virgin Islands in 1917!

clues.stem: Before or After in Capital Moves: Which country moved its seat of government to a new purpose-built city FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Kazakhstan shifted from Almaty to Astana in December 1997—eight years before Myanmar relocated to Naypyidaw in 2005!

clues.stem: Before or After in Cartography: Which landmark map projection or atlas was published EARLIER?
clues.ahaFactoid: Gerardus Mercator published his navigation-friendly 1569 wall map—over two centuries before Mollweide (1805) and Robinson (1963)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Time Zones: Which Pacific time-zone quirk happened MORE RECENTLY—Samoa skipping Friday Dec 30 or Kiribati jumping to UTC+14?
clues.ahaFactoid: Kiribati shifted east across the Date Line ahead of 1995, while Samoa skipped December 30, 2011 to align its business week with Sydney!

clues.stem: Before or After in Canadian Maps: Which territorial milestone happened FIRST—Nunavut's creation or the Confederation Bridge opening?
clues.ahaFactoid: Yukon Territory formed in 1898, Newfoundland joined Canada in 1949, Confederation Bridge opened in 1997, and Nunavut launched in 1999!

clues.stem: Why does Paris's wrought-iron Eiffel Tower actually stand up to six inches TALLER on hot July afternoons than in January?
clues.ahaFactoid: Warm summer sun heats its 7,300 tons of puddle iron, causing the lattice frame to expand skyward—and lean slightly away from the sun!

clues.stem: Which snowy, cherry-blossom-lined country calls itself "Nihon" or "Nippon"—literally translating to "Origin of the Sun"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ancient Chinese neighbors called the islands to their east the "Land of the Rising Sun"—hence the glowing red sun disc on Japan's flag!

clues.stem: Carving mile-deep red rock gorges across northern Arizona over millions of years, which mighty river flows along the Grand Canyon floor?
clues.ahaFactoid: The Grand Canyon spans 277 river miles and hides roughly two billion years of Earth's rock layers in its striped walls!

clues.stem: Theme park fans know "Six Flags" comes from history: how many sovereign nations (including the Republic of Texas) ruled Texas soil?
clues.ahaFactoid: Spain, France, Mexico, the Republic of Texas, the Confederacy, and the United States all flew banners over Texas!

clues.stem: Mocked in 1867 newspapers as a frozen "polar bear garden" bought from Russia for two cents an acre, the Alaska deal earned what famous nickname?
clues.ahaFactoid: Russia's $7.2 million deal quickly looked like the bargain of the century once Klondike gold and North Slope oil turned up!

clues.stem: Stand with one sneaker in the Eastern Hemisphere and one in the West at the Royal Observatory in which world capital?
clues.ahaFactoid: Greenwich in southeast London marks 0° longitude, where sailors set chronometers to Greenwich Mean Time for centuries!

clues.stem: Why do Colorado and Wyoming stand out as neat four-sided shapes on U.S. road atlases? Their borders follow straight lines of what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Wait—because Earth is curved, those parallel meridian sides slightly taper north, making Colorado actually have 697 tiny survey kinks!

clues.stem: Texas is so huge that west-corner El Paso actually sits closer to San Diego, California than to which Gulf-side Texas city?
clues.ahaFactoid: El Paso to San Diego is roughly 725 miles, while driving east from El Paso to Houston or Beaumont stretches 750 to 830 miles!

clues.stem: Look across every UN member banner waving in New York: which island nation flies the ONLY national flag with ZERO red, white, or blue?
clues.ahaFactoid: Featuring a bold gold diagonal cross over black and green triangles, Jamaica's 1962 flag skips red, white, and blue completely!

clues.stem: Since 1931, a granite obelisk in the small town of Rugby has boasted marking the geographic center of North America in which state?
clues.ahaFactoid: A 2015 study nudged the exact centroid slightly west to tiny Center, North Dakota, though Rugby still guards the classic monument!

clues.stem: Which chalk-cliffed European strait narrows to just 21 miles between England and France—close enough for marathon swimmers?
clues.ahaFactoid: Matthew Webb became the first person to swim the Strait of Dover unassisted in 1875, battling jellyfish and tides for nearly 22 hours!

clues.stem: Tucked between giants Brazil and Argentina on the Rio de la Plata estuary, which South American nation calls seaside Montevideo home?
clues.ahaFactoid: Host and champion of the inaugural 1930 FIFA World Cup, Uruguay's flag shares a smiling Sun of May with neighbor Argentina!

clues.stem: Highway Dispatch: Stretching 2,448 miles from Chicago diners to Santa Monica Pier, John Steinbeck dubbed U.S. Route 66 [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: In The Grapes of Wrath, Steinbeck christened Highway 66 "the path of a people in flight"—and the nickname stuck for good!

clues.stem: Southern Courthouse Wire: While 48 states divide into counties and Alaska uses boroughs, Louisiana splits its map into 64 [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Inherited from Spanish and French Catholic church districts, Louisiana parishes work just like counties in state government!

clues.stem: 1520 Ship Log: Surviving stormy Patagonia straits to enter calm open waters, Ferdinand Magellan named the vast ocean [ _____ ] ("Peaceful").
clues.ahaFactoid: Covering one-third of Earth's surface, the Pacific is big enough to swallow every single continent on the planet with room to spare!

clues.stem: Boulevard Wire: Famous both for early gas streetlamps and Enlightenment thinkers, travelers affectionately call Paris the [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: French "La Ville Lumiere" originally honored Paris's scholars and philosophers—only later gaining sparkle from 56,000 streetlamps!

clues.stem: Shipping Desk: Linking Port Said to Suez, Egypt's 120-mile desert canal saves freighters a 5,500-mile Africa detour by joining the Red Sea to the [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Around 12% of global seaborne trade squeezes through that single 120-mile desert trench every year!

clues.stem: 1836 Border Deal: To end the bloodless "Toledo War" with Ohio over a port strip, Congress handed Michigan the copper-rich [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Michigan thought it lost the trade at the time—until massive iron and copper veins turned the Upper Peninsula into a jackpot!

clues.stem: Arabian Gulf Wire: Connected to Saudi Arabia by a 16-mile concrete causeway, the island kingdom of [ _____ ] ranks among Asia's tiniest nations.
clues.ahaFactoid: Centered around a 30-island archipelago, Bahrain's name literally means "Two Seas" in Arabic!

clues.stem: Polar Accord Wire: Signed by twelve nations in 1959, the [ _____ ] Treaty bans mining and military bases across Earth's frozen south.
clues.ahaFactoid: Signed in 1959 at the height of the Cold War, the treaty preserves an entire frozen continent strictly for peaceful science!

clues.stem: Maritime Chokepoint: Funneling over 80,000 cargo vessels yearly between Malaysia and Sumatra, the [ _____ ] links India's waters to China's.
clues.ahaFactoid: Squeezing down to just 1.7 miles wide near Singapore, the Strait of Malacca is one of the busiest shipping lanes on Earth!

clues.stem: 1859 Biogeography Wire: Running between Bali and Lombok, the [ _____ ] splits Asian monkeys from Australian cockatoos and marsupials.
clues.ahaFactoid: Deep ocean trenches between Bali and Lombok never dried up even during Ice Ages, keeping two evolutionary worlds miles apart!

clues.stem: Look at Europe's coastline on the Monitor: one Mediterranean peninsula looks unmistakably like a high-heeled leather boot kicking what island?
clues.ahaFactoid: Sicily sits just two miles off Italy's "toe" across the narrow Strait of Messina—close enough to swim on a calm day!

clues.stem: Zoom in on Britain's Union Jack: its red-and-white diagonal and upright crosses blend St. George of England, St. Andrew of Scotland, and who?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because Wales was already legally united with England back in 1536, the Welsh red dragon never got added to the Union Jack!

clues.stem: Spot the crisp green tree centered inside a white stripe between two crimson bars on the flag of which Middle Eastern nation?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ancient Phoenicians built royal fleets and Solomon's Temple timber out of towering Mount Lebanon cedar trees!

clues.stem: On the Monitor: A brass mariner's compass rose prints N, E, S, and W clockwise. Which cardinal point sits directly at 270 degrees?
clues.ahaFactoid: North is 0° (or 360°), East is 90°, South is 180°, and West sits cleanly at 270°—remember "Never Eat Soggy Waffles" clockwise!

clues.stem: Picture Brazil's green-and-yellow banner centering a starry blue globe: its curved white ribbon motto "Ordem e Progresso" means what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Inspired by philosopher Auguste Comte's positivism, the starry sky depicts Rio de Janeiro's stars on November 15, 1889!

clues.stem: Examine Washington, D.C.'s map silhouette: originally laid out as a neat 10-by-10-mile diamond, why does its southwest wedge look missing?
clues.ahaFactoid: In 1846 Congress retroceded Alexandria and Arlington back to Virginia, leaving D.C. wholly on the Maryland side of the Potomac!

clues.stem: Hold a ruler to the Monitor: among all UN member states, only Vatican City and which Alpine country fly a perfectly SQUARE banner?
clues.ahaFactoid: That crisp white cross on a 1:1 crimson square later inspired the inverted Red Cross emblem founded in Geneva in 1863!

clues.stem: Look at Oklahoma's skinny western Panhandle sticking out like a frying-pan handle: why was that 166-mile strip once called "No Man's Land"?
clues.ahaFactoid: When Texas gave up land north of 36°30' and Kansas stopped at 37°N, a 34-mile orphan strip sat without any state government for 40 years!

clues.stem: Spot the orange copper-colored island silhouette cradled above twin olive branches on the national flag of which Mediterranean republic?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cyprus is one of the only national flags on Earth—alongside Kosovo—displaying an exact geographic map silhouette of its own country!

clues.stem: On the Monitor: A blazing gold sun radiates 40 rays around crossed wooden yurt roof poles (tunduk) on the red banner of which Central Asian nation?
clues.ahaFactoid: Its 40 golden rays celebrate the 40 nomadic clans united by legendary Kyrgyz epic hero Manas!

clues.stem: Travel Klaxon! Three of these world-weather claims hold up, while one desert-heat assumption melts under thermometer data. Spot the myth!
clues.ahaFactoid: Equatorial rainforests stay humid and cloudy near 85-90°F—Earth's deadliest heatwaves roast subtropical deserts like Death Valley and Iran's Lut!

clues.stem: Atlas Klaxon! Three of these landmark facts check out, while one popular claim about China's Great Wall misreads aerial reality!
clues.ahaFactoid: Rather than one continuous ribbon, the Great Wall is an overlapping network of Ming, Han, and Qin walls, natural cliffs, and watchtowers!

clues.stem: Japan Desk Klaxon! Three of these island facts are true, while one mixes up Edo with Japan's ancient imperial seat for over a millennium!
clues.ahaFactoid: Kyoto served as Japan's imperial capital from 794 to 1868—when Emperor Meiji moved east to Edo and renamed it Tokyo ("Eastern Capital")!

clues.stem: North America Klaxon! Three of these border facts are rock-solid, while one civic claim mixes up Canada's biggest metropolis with its true political capital!
clues.ahaFactoid: Queen Victoria chose riverfront Ottawa—sitting right on the English-French border between Ontario and Quebec—as Canada's capital in 1857!

clues.stem: Nordic Klaxon! Three of these polar facts are true, while one mixes up the snowy reality of Greenland and green coastal Iceland!
clues.ahaFactoid: Only about 11% of Iceland wears glaciers—while Greenland wears a giant ice cap up to two miles thick!

clues.stem: Monument Klaxon! Three of these Statue of Liberty facts are 100% genuine, while one misses how shiny she looked in 1886!
clues.ahaFactoid: Lady Liberty stands on Liberty Island (formerly Bedloe's Island)—neighbors with Ellis Island, which sits in New York/New Jersey waters!

clues.stem: Rainforest Klaxon! Three of these Amazon facts check out, while one highway fantasy clashes with the river's soggy floodplains!
clues.ahaFactoid: Zero bridges cross the main stem of the Amazon—seasonal floods swell the banks miles wide, so travelers rely entirely on ferries!

clues.stem: Compass Klaxon! Three of these Panama Canal facts are true, while one intuitive compass guess gets turned upside-down by the isthmus!
choices: Pacific exit lies west of Atlantic
Pacific exit lies east of Atlantic
clues.ahaFactoid: Because Panama's S-curve bends sharply, ships sailing from the Atlantic TO the Pacific actually travel SOUTHEAST!

clues.stem: Projection Klaxon! Three of these world-area comparisons are true, while one Mercator-warped belief shrinks an entire continent!
clues.ahaFactoid: Mercator maps stretch northern Russia huge—in reality Africa (11.7M sq mi) is nearly 1.8 times the size of Russia (6.6M sq mi)!

clues.stem: Capitals Klaxon! Three of these sovereign-capital quirks are true, while one claims a triple-capital powerhouse only runs one city!
clues.ahaFactoid: South Africa famously splits power across Pretoria (executive), Cape Town (legislative), and Bloemfontein (judicial)!

clues.stem: 50/50 Compass Bet: Look at a true U.S. longitude map—which city actually sits farther WEST, Reno, Nevada or Los Angeles, California?
clues.ahaFactoid: California's coastline angles steeply southeast—putting Reno (119.8°W) clearly west of Los Angeles (118.2°W)!

clues.stem: 50/50 Polar Reality: Beneath the shifting sea ice at the North Pole, do explorers stand over solid rock continent or deep Arctic Ocean?
clues.ahaFactoid: Unlike mountainous Antarctica, the geographic North Pole floats over more than 13,000 feet of icy Arctic Ocean!

clues.stem: 50/50 Border Check: Cross the Ambassador Bridge from Detroit, Michigan into Windsor, Ontario—which compass direction do you drive?
clues.ahaFactoid: A sharp bend in the Detroit River puts Windsor directly south of downtown Detroit—the classic U.S.-Canada bar-bet trick!

clues.stem: 50/50 Globe Test: Does roughly 90% of the human population live north of the Equator or south of the Equator?
clues.ahaFactoid: Almost all of North America, Europe, Asia, and two-thirds of Africa pack above the Equator!

clues.stem: 50/50 Scale Shock: At its widest stretch from Indonesia to Colombia, is the Pacific Ocean wider or narrower than the entire Moon's diameter?
clues.ahaFactoid: Stretching roughly 12,300 miles across, the Pacific easily dwarfs the Moon's 2,159-mile diameter more than five times over!

clues.stem: 50/50 Atlas Surprise: Does South America lie mostly EAST or mostly WEST of Florida's Miami longitude (80°W)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Wait—even Lima, Peru (77°W) sits EAST of Miami (80°W), and eastern Brazil reaches 35°W, way out toward Africa!

clues.stem: 50/50 Physics Map: Does Earth's Coriolis spin actually force everyday household sink drains to swirl opposite ways across the Equator?
clues.ahaFactoid: Coriolis acceleration is millions of times too weak for a sink—pipe jets and bowl symmetry dictate the swirl, while hurricanes obey Coriolis!

clues.stem: 50/50 Border Oddity: Does Russian exclave Kaliningrad sit physically attached to mainland Russia or tucked between Poland and Lithuania?
clues.ahaFactoid: Formerly German Koenigsberg—home to mathematician Euler's Seven Bridges puzzle—Kaliningrad became a Baltic Russian exclave after 1945!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on the Hardwood: Which official playing-field target sits HIGHER above the ground?
clues.ahaFactoid: James Naismith nailed his original peach baskets onto a 10-foot Springfield gym balcony in 1891—and the height never budged!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on Scorecards: Which iconic single-game maximum or par benchmark is a HIGHER number?
clues.ahaFactoid: Rolling 12 straight strikes delivers a spotless 300 in ten-pin bowling—dwarfing a 147 maximum snooker break!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on Roster Count: Which pro sport puts MORE players from one team on the live playing surface at once?
clues.ahaFactoid: Soccer fields 11 per side, beating baseball's 9 defenders, hockey's 6 skaters, and basketball's 5!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in MLB History: Which franchise has captured MORE World Series championships?
clues.ahaFactoid: The New York Yankees own 27 World Series titles—more than double runner-up St. Louis's 11 championships!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in NBA Championships: Which Hall of Fame legend won MORE NBA title rings as a player?
clues.ahaFactoid: Boston Celtics center Bill Russell collected an untouched 11 NBA rings in 13 seasons—even winning his last two as player-coach!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on the Gridiron: Which NFL scoring play puts MORE points on the scoreboard?
clues.ahaFactoid: A touchdown pays 6 points (double a 3-point field goal)—though back in 1883, a touchdown only counted 4 points!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Olympic Lore: Which superstar won MORE career Olympic gold medals?
clues.ahaFactoid: Swimmer Mark Spitz famously swept 7 golds at Munich 1972 alone—adding two relay golds from 1968 to reach 9 total!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Golf Scoring: Which score on a par-4 hole gives you a LOWER (better) stroke count?
clues.ahaFactoid: Draining your approach shot in two strokes on a par-4 scores a thrilling Eagle (2-under par)!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on the Diamond: Which distance on an MLB field is LONGER?
clues.ahaFactoid: A baseball diamond places bases 90 feet apart, whereas the pitcher's rubber sits 60 feet 6 inches from home plate!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower at One Grand Slam: Which single-tournament tennis title record stands HIGHER?
clues.ahaFactoid: Rafael Nadal went 112-4 on Roland-Garros red clay to hoist an unreal 14 Musketeers' Cups!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in MLB Sluggers: Who finished his career with MORE official regular-season home runs?
clues.ahaFactoid: Barry Bonds finished at 762 career home runs, edging Hank Aaron (755) and Babe Ruth (714)!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Unbroken Streaks: Which legendary streak lasted MORE consecutive games or matches?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cal Ripken Jr. played an ironman 2,632 consecutive MLB games from 1982 to 1998—eclipsing Lou Gehrig's 2,130!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in FIFA World Cups: Which men's national team has lifted the World Cup trophy MORE times?
clues.ahaFactoid: Brazil holds five men's World Cup crowns (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002), one ahead of four-time winners Germany and Italy!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Pro Scoring: Who racked up MORE career NHL regular-season goals?
clues.ahaFactoid: Washington Capitals captain Alex Ovechkin eclipsed Wayne Gretzky's 894-goal NHL record in April 2025!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Pro Gear: Which official regulation game ball weighs MORE on a locker-room scale?
clues.ahaFactoid: An official NBA leather basketball tops 22 ounces—noticeably heavier than a FIFA soccer ball or NFL pigskin!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Single-Game Scoring: Which NBA total sits SECOND ALL-TIME behind Wilt Chamberlain's 100?
clues.ahaFactoid: Kobe Bryant poured in 81 points against Toronto in January 2006—shooting 28-of-46 from the floor and 18-of-20 at the line!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Cycling: Which Grand Tour covers roughly 2,100 miles across MORE days of racing each summer—or are all three 21 stages?
clues.ahaFactoid: Every modern men's Grand Tour (Tour de France, Giro d'Italia, Vuelta a Espana) standardizes around 21 racing stages plus two rest days!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in College Hoops: Which legendary coach won MORE Division I men's or women's NCAA basketball titles?
clues.ahaFactoid: UConn's Geno Auriemma captured his 12th NCAA crown in 2025, topping UCLA legend John Wooden's 10 men's titles!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower at Wimbledon: How many total games were played in the 2010 Isner-Mahut three-day marathon match?
clues.ahaFactoid: John Isner finally defeated Nicolas Mahut 70-68 in the fifth set after 11 hours and 5 minutes—forcing Wimbledon to adopt final-set tiebreaks!
