clues.stem: Olympia Wire: Months before every Opening Ceremony, priestesses ignite the official Olympic flame using only a parabolic mirror and [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: If clouds hide the sun on ceremony day, officials pull out a backup flame lit during dress rehearsal by pure sunbeams days earlier!

clues.stem: Basketball Wire: Sweeping gracefully across his body with outstretched long arms, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar made the [ _____ ] virtually unblockable.
clues.ahaFactoid: Kareem perfected that ambidextrous hook in high school drills because strict NCAA rules briefly banned dunking during his UCLA years!

clues.stem: Premier League Wire: When a goalkeeper finishes ninety minutes without allowing a single goal, British broadcasters hail a [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Old-school reporters recorded goals on crisp paper sheets—so zero goals against left the opponent's side of the page literally clean!

clues.stem: Bronx Wire, Oct 1956: Yankees pitcher [ _____ ] retired all 27 Brooklyn Dodgers in Game 5—still the only perfect game in World Series history.
clues.ahaFactoid: Larsen threw only 97 pitches in his no-windup delivery—and Yogi Berra leaped straight into his chest on the final called third strike!

clues.stem: Frozen Tundra Wire, Dec 1967: At minus-13°F wind chills where whistles froze to lips, Bart Starr sneaked in to win the [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Cowboys and Packers played over frozen tundra after Lambeau Field's brand-new electric turf heating coils snapped under frost!

clues.stem: Look at the five interlocking Olympic rings on the Monitor: blue, black, red, yellow, and green were chosen so every flag in 1913 had at least one color on what field?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pierre de Coubertin noted in 1913 that those five ring hues plus the white canvas represented every single competing nation's banner!

clues.stem: Zoom in on an official Major League baseball's raised crimson seams: how many double red stitches hold its two figure-eight cowhide covers tight?
clues.ahaFactoid: Workers hand-stitch all 108 double seams with waxed red cotton thread—giving pitchers grip to bend curveballs and sliders!

clues.stem: Spot the iconic red-white-and-blue MLB batter silhouette on caps: which Minnesota Twins slugger inspired designer Jerry Dior's 1968 emblem?
clues.ahaFactoid: Dior later insisted he drew a composite hitter rather than one man—yet Killebrew swore the stance matched his own famous swing!

clues.stem: Picture hockey's towering three-foot silver Stanley Cup: unlike other pro trophies, what gets stamped straight onto its removable silver bands each year?
clues.ahaFactoid: When all five lower rings fill up every 13 seasons, the oldest ring retires to the Hockey Hall of Fame in Toronto to make room!

clues.stem: Inspect a golf ball under studio lights: why do manufacturers mold 300 to 500 tiny circular dimples across its shell instead of keeping it glass-smooth?
clues.ahaFactoid: Smooth golf balls travel barely half as far—dimples create a thin turbulent air layer that lets drives soar cleanly through the breeze!

clues.stem: Peek closely at the very top of Wimbledon's gleaming silver Men's Singles Challenge Cup: what quirky tropical fruit sits sculpted as the finial?
clues.ahaFactoid: In 1887 Victorian London, pineapples were jaw-dropping status symbols of luxury—explaining why one still crowns tennis's oldest trophy!

clues.stem: Look at college football's bronze Heisman statue: which 1935 Chicago Maroons halfback won the very FIRST trophy—and let his aunt use it as a doorstop?
clues.ahaFactoid: Berwanger skipped the NFL entirely to sell foam rubber and plastics—leaving his historic 1935 trophy holding open his aunt's parlor door!

clues.stem: Zoom into Fenway Park's right-field foul corner: only 302 feet from home plate, the bright yellow foul pole honors which beloved Red Sox infielder?
clues.ahaFactoid: Teammate Mel Parnell nicknamed it "Pesky's Pole" after light-hitting Johnny Pesky curled a rare walk-off homer right around it in 1948!

clues.stem: Spot the original solid-gold World Cup (Jules Rimet Trophy) lifted from 1930 to 1970: a winged Greek Victory statue held an octagonal cup before what fate?
clues.ahaFactoid: After Brazil kept it permanently in 1970, thieves pried open a Rio display cabinet in 1983 and likely melted it down—never recovered!

clues.stem: Inspect the French Open men's silver trophy topped with swan handles: Coupe des Mousquetaires honors how many 1920s French tennis legends?
clues.ahaFactoid: René Lacoste, Jean Borotra, Henri Cochet, and Jacques Brugnon swept six straight Davis Cups—inspiring both the trophy and Lacoste's croc shirt!

clues.stem: Locker Room Klaxon! Three of these sports gear facts are 100% genuine, while one popular nickname fools fans about what an NFL ball is made of!
clues.ahaFactoid: Modern NFL footballs are stitched from pebbled Horween COWHIDE—early 1860s bladders were sometimes inflated pig bladders, leaving the nickname behind!

clues.stem: Hardwood Klaxon! Three of these hoops origin facts check out, while one tall tale claims James Naismith's very first games used wire rims and glass boards!
clues.ahaFactoid: No glass in 1891! Backboards were first added in 1893 out of wire mesh just to keep rowdy balcony spectators from swatting shots away!

clues.stem: Dugout Klaxon! Three of these classic baseball stories hold up, while one fashion rumor claims the Yankees added pinstripes just to slim down Babe Ruth!
clues.ahaFactoid: The Yankees first wore pinstripes in 1912 and permanently in 1915—years BEFORE Babe Ruth arrived from Boston in 1920!

clues.stem: Umpire Klaxon! Three of these quirky baseball truths are real rules, while one famous basepath cliché isn't written anywhere in MLB rules!
clues.ahaFactoid: The MLB rulebook explicitly says the runner must BEAT the ball to first base—if it's a literal tie, the runner didn't beat it, though umps call safe!

clues.stem: Stadium Klaxon! Three of these world sports facts check out, while one popular assumption about Sumo wrestling invents fake weight classes!
clues.ahaFactoid: Grand Sumo has ZERO weight classes and ZERO weight minimum—lean 215-pound technicians regularly topple 400-pound giants with throws!

clues.stem: Hoop Lore Klaxon! Three of these NBA stories are true, while one famous legend about 15-year-old Michael Jordan leaves out a huge detail!
clues.ahaFactoid: Jordan wasn't kicked out of basketball—Coach Pop Herring put sophomore Mike on JV (over 6'7" friend Leroy Smith) so he'd actually play every minute!

clues.stem: Olympic Klaxon! Three of these Olympic tidbits are true, while one forgets that early modern Games awarded actual gold medals to painters and poets!
choices: Tug of War was an Olympic event
clues.ahaFactoid: Even before Dream Team pros arrived in 1992, Baron de Coubertin handed Olympic medals for architecture, sculpture, music, and poetry until 1948!

clues.stem: Fenway Klaxon! Three of these baseball history facts are true, while one famous curse rumor gets the exact Broadway musical wrong by years!
choices: Red Sox sold Ruth in Dec 1919
clues.ahaFactoid: Harry Frazee sold Babe Ruth to finance My Lady Friends in 1920—five full years BEFORE No, No, Nanette even opened on Broadway!

clues.stem: Track Klaxon! Three of these absurd 1904 St. Louis Olympic Marathon tales really happened, while one neat claim about smooth paved air-conditioned triumph is pure fiction!
clues.ahaFactoid: Not only did Fred Lorz ride 11 miles in his manager's car, official pace vehicles kicked up choking dust clouds that sent a runner to the hospital!

clues.stem: Rulebook Klaxon! Three of these bizarre pro-sport rules are real, while one denies a referee's rare power to award an automatic touchdown!
choices: NBA shooter can dunk free throws
Ref can award TD on unfair play
clues.ahaFactoid: Under NFL Rule 12-3-4 (Palpably Unfair Act), if a bench player tackles a breakaway runner, the referee can literally award a touchdown!

clues.stem: 50/50 Diamond Direction: After cracking a base hit in Baseball, which way do runners circle the four bases—counterclockwise or clockwise?
clues.ahaFactoid: Early 1845 Knickerbocker Rules locked in counterclockwise running—making left-handed hitters one big step closer to first base!

clues.stem: 50/50 Podium Check: Are modern Summer Olympic "gold" medals minted mostly out of solid gold or sterling silver plated with pure gold?
clues.ahaFactoid: Solid gold medals ended after Stockholm 1912—modern Olympic golds are ~92.5% sterling silver coated with at least 6 grams of 24k gold!

clues.stem: 50/50 Clock Check: Does men's NCAA Division I college basketball play four 10-minute quarters or two 20-minute halves?
clues.ahaFactoid: While women's college basketball switched to four 10-minute quarters in 2015, men's NCAA hoops still plays two 20-minute halves!

clues.stem: 50/50 Scoring Call: Reaching 40-40 (Deuce) in a standard Tennis game, how many consecutive points must a player win from Deuce to take the game?
clues.ahaFactoid: Winning one point gives you Advantage—you need the very next point too, or it snaps right back to Deuce!

clues.stem: 50/50 Umpire Call: If a tapped MLB bunt lands cleanly ON the white chalk of the first-base line and stops there, is it fair or foul?
clues.ahaFactoid: The white chalk lines—and home plate itself—belong strictly to FAIR territory, just like a soccer ball or tennis ball kissing the line!

clues.stem: 50/50 Pitch Rules: If a fierce corner-area shot bounces off the corner flagstick or referee and stays on the grass, is play still LIVE?
clues.ahaFactoid: Corner flags and goalposts count as live pitch fixtures—if the ball hits them and stays inbounds, play keeps rolling!

clues.stem: 50/50 Links Rulebook: Under modern 2019 Golf rules, does putting on the green with the flagstick LEFT IN the hole trigger a two-stroke penalty?
clues.ahaFactoid: Until 2019, hitting an unattended flagstick from the green cost two strokes—today pros like Bryson DeChambeau leave it in on purpose!

clues.stem: 50/50 Baseball Rulebook: When an ambidextrous pitcher faces a switch-hitter, who must declare which side they're throwing/batting from FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: After switch-pitcher Pat Venditte and switch-hitter Ralph Henriquez danced back and forth in 2008, MLB wrote the "Venditte Rule" forcing the pitcher to pick first!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower on the British Throne: Which monarch reigned MORE total years over the United Kingdom?
clues.ahaFactoid: Reigning 70 years and 214 days (1952-2022), Elizabeth II surpassed Victoria's 63-year mark in September 2015!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Tudor Courts: How many official wives did King Henry VIII marry in his lifetime?
clues.ahaFactoid: Remember their fates with the classic rhyme: Divorced, Beheaded, Died, Divorced, Beheaded, Survived!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in 1776 Philadelphia: How many delegates signed the Declaration of Independence?
clues.ahaFactoid: 56 delegates signed the 1776 Declaration, while 39 signed the U.S. Constitution eleven years later in 1787!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Royal Reigns: Who ruled longer—France's Sun King Louis XIV or Britain's Elizabeth II?
clues.ahaFactoid: Crowned at age four in 1643, Louis XIV holds the longest verified reign of any sovereign European monarch at 72 years and 110 days!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Early U.S. Counts: Which Founding-era count was LARGER?
clues.ahaFactoid: Thirteen colonies signed on in 1776, whereas James Madison's original 12 proposed amendments trimmed down to 10 ratified in 1791!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Time Gaps: Which span of years was LONGER?
clues.ahaFactoid: Khufu's Great Pyramid rose ~2560 BCE—over 2,500 years before Cleopatra, compared to just ~2,000 years from Cleopatra to Apollo 11!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Territorial Empires: Which empire ruled MORE contiguous square miles of connected land?
clues.ahaFactoid: Covering 9.3 million contiguous square miles from Korea to Poland, the Mongol domain dwarfed Rome's ~1.9 million square miles!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Ancient Counts: Which Roman or Mediterranean number is HIGHER?
clues.ahaFactoid: Engraved in bronze around 450 BCE, the Twelve Tables posted Rome's public laws in the Forum so plebeians could read their rights!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Royal Ages: Roughly how old was Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun when he died?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ascending the throne around age 9 and dying around 19, the Boy King's rushed small tomb accidentally hid his treasure for 3,200 years!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in U.S. Birthplaces: Which state gave birth to MORE U.S. Presidents?
clues.ahaFactoid: Virginia earned "Mother of Presidents" with Washington, Jefferson, Madison, Monroe, W.H. Harrison, Tyler, Taylor, and Wilson!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Dynasty Longevity: Which famous imperial house ruled continuously for MORE centuries?
clues.ahaFactoid: Founded by Osman I around 1299 and lasting until 1922, the Ottoman dynasty spanned 623 years across three continents!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Ancient Egypt: Roughly how many years did pharaoh Ramesses II rule Egypt?
clues.ahaFactoid: Living past age 90, Ramesses the Great outlived several of his own heirs and fathered roughly 100 sons and daughters!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Founding Ink: How many essays make up The Federalist Papers written by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay?
clues.ahaFactoid: Alexander Hamilton penned 51 of the 85 essays, James Madison wrote 29, and an illness-sidelined John Jay contributed 5!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Royal Lineages: Which existing monarchy claims the LONGEST unbroken hereditary line in history?
clues.ahaFactoid: Historically documented since Emperor Kinmei in the 500s CE (and traditionally back to 660 BCE), Japan's imperial line is unmatched!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Edo Japan: Roughly how long did the Tokugawa Shogunate keep Japan unified and largely at peace?
clues.ahaFactoid: From Ieyasu's 1603 appointment until the 1868 Meiji Restoration, 15 Tokugawa shoguns presided over Japan's bustling Edo Period!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Ancient China: Which unified imperial dynasty lasted LONGER on the dragon throne?
clues.ahaFactoid: Like the 37-year Sui before Tang, the harsh Qin lasted only 15 years yet built China's blueprint for the 400-year Han!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Norse History: From the 793 Lindisfarne raid to 1066 Stamford Bridge, roughly how many years lasted the Viking Age?
clues.ahaFactoid: Nearly three centuries of longships carried Norse traders and raiders from Newfoundland to Constantinople and Baghdad!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Conquerors: How old was Alexander the Great when he died in Babylon in 323 BCE?
clues.ahaFactoid: In just thirteen years on the throne, Alexander marched his army over 11,000 miles from Greece to the Indus River without losing a pitched battle!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Constantinople: Who reigned MORE years over the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ruling solely for 49 years (976 to 1025), austere soldier-emperor Basil II topped Justinian's 38 years and left the treasury overflowing!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Mughal India: Which Gunpowder-Era emperor ruled MORE consecutive years on the Delhi throne?
clues.ahaFactoid: Grandfather Akbar (1556-1605) and great-grandson Aurangzeb (1658-1707) remarkably both ruled for 49 years—ahead of Shah Jahan's 30!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Verified Reigns: King Sobhuza II of Eswatini holds the longest verified reign of a sovereign monarch—roughly how long?
clues.ahaFactoid: Proclaimed king at just four months old in December 1899, Sobhuza II ruled until August 1982—longer than Louis XIV or Elizabeth II!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower in Egyptian Queens: The famous Cleopatra was actually Cleopatra VII—how many numbered Cleopatras came BEFORE her in Ptolemy Egypt?
clues.ahaFactoid: And unlike the 14 Greek-speaking Ptolemies before her, Cleopatra VII was the very first ruler in her dynasty to bother learning native Egyptian!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on Mount Rushmore: Three of these Americans are carved in 60-foot granite faces, while one Founding Father is NOT!
clues.ahaFactoid: Mount Rushmore's quartet is Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Lincoln—leaving witty Ben Franklin on the $100 bill instead!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in White House History: Three of these Founding Fathers served as U.S. President, while one Treasury boss NEVER did!
clues.ahaFactoid: Born in Nevis in the Caribbean, first Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton shaped U.S. finance—and died in an 1804 duel!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Ancient Rulers: Three of these ruled Egypt as Pharaoh, while one was the Roman general who defeated Hannibal!
clues.ahaFactoid: Scipio Africanus shattered Carthaginian power at Zama in 202 BCE, earning his famous Africanus victory surname in Rome!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Viking Homelands: Three of these modern Nordic countries were classic Viking homelands, while one lies sunny and Mediterranean!
clues.ahaFactoid: Though Vikings raided Iberian coasts, the Norse homelands centered in Norway, Sweden, and Denmark!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Warrior Traditions: Three of these belong to classic Japanese Samurai lore, while one was England's deadly medieval bow!
clues.ahaFactoid: Carved six feet tall from yew wood, the English longbow shattered French knight charges at Crecy and Agincourt!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in English Royal Houses: Three of these monarchs belonged to the House of Tudor, while one hailed from Hanover!
clues.ahaFactoid: The Tudor dynasty spanned 1485 to 1603—over a century before Hanoverian King George III lost the American colonies!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Versailles Lore: Three of these monarchs ruled France as "Louis," while one ruled England before losing his head!
clues.ahaFactoid: England executed Stuart King Charles I in 1649—144 years before French revolutionaries guillotined Louis XVI in 1793!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in U.S. Currency: Three of these Founding Fathers grace everyday American paper bills, while one NEVER appeared on circulating notes!
clues.ahaFactoid: Washington ($1), Jefferson ($2), and Hamilton ($10) grace circulating bills—while 2nd President John Adams never got his own paper note!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Antiquity: Three of these men ruled as Roman Emperors, while one marched war elephants FROM Carthage against Rome!
clues.ahaFactoid: Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the icy Alps in 218 BCE to battle the Roman Republic—centuries before emperors took over!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on the Calendar: Three English weekdays honor Norse/Germanic figures (Tyr, Odin, Thor), while one honors a Roman planet!
clues.ahaFactoid: Tuesday (Tyr), Wednesday (Woden/Odin), Thursday (Thor), and Friday (Frigg) stay Norse—while Saturday salutes Roman Saturn!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Royal Palaces: Three of these belong to the British Crown, while one sparkles outside Paris!
clues.ahaFactoid: Transformed from a royal hunting lodge by Louis XIV, Versailles gleams with 357 mirrors in its Hall of Mirrors—12 miles southwest of Paris!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Henry VIII's Court: Three of these women married King Henry VIII, while one was his fierce Catholic daughter!
clues.ahaFactoid: Daughter of Catherine of Aragon, Mary I became England's first crowned queen regnant in 1553—before half-sister Elizabeth I!

clues.stem: Odd One Out on the Ides of March: Three of these Romans plotted Julius Caesar's assassination, while one delivered his fierce funeral speech!
clues.ahaFactoid: Mark Antony stayed loyal to Caesar—rallying Rome against the conspirators before teaming with Cleopatra in Egypt!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in East Asian Eras: Three of these are classic Chinese imperial dynasties, while one modernized Japan in 1868!
clues.ahaFactoid: Restoring imperial rule in 1868, Japan's Meiji Era turned feudal samurai domains into a steam-and-railroad industrial power in one generation!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Rome's Golden Age: Three belong to Machiavelli's "Five Good Emperors," while one gladiator-obsessed son broke the streak!
clues.ahaFactoid: Breaking five consecutive peaceful adoptions, Marcus Aurelius handed Rome to his biological son Commodus—kicking off decades of chaos!

clues.stem: Odd One Out After Alexander: Three of these dynasties were founded by Alexander the Great's Macedonian generals, while one rose from Iranian nomads!
clues.ahaFactoid: The horse-archers of Parthia carved Persia out of the Seleucid Empire and later crushed Roman legions at Carrhae!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Royal Houses: Three of these dynasties reigned over medieval or early-modern France, while one reigned over England!
clues.ahaFactoid: Though French-speaking Plantagenets originally hailed from Anjou, they wore the English crown for over 330 years from 1154 to 1485!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in the Americas: Three of these cultures thrived in Mesoamerica (Mexico/Central America), while one ruled South America's Andes!
clues.ahaFactoid: Centered in Cusco, Peru, the Inca Empire built roughly 25,000 miles of stone mountain roads across the Andes!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Japanese Unifiers: Three warlords forged unified 16th-century Japan, while one founded the 1192 Kamakura Shogunate!
clues.ahaFactoid: Minamoto Yoritomo claimed the title of Seii Taishogun four centuries earlier in 1192 after winning the Genpei War!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in African Empires: Three of these gold-and-salt empires rose across West Africa, while one flourished in Ethiopia!
clues.ahaFactoid: Straddling the Red Sea trade routes from Ethiopia to Yemen, Aksum minted its own gold coins and raised towering granite stelae!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Mesopotamia: Three of these monarchs ruled Babylon, while one forged the much earlier Akkadian Empire!
clues.ahaFactoid: Ruling around 2334 BCE, Sargon of Akkad united Sumerian city-states into history's first multi-ethnic empire centuries before Babylon peaked!

clues.stem: Odd One Out in Habsburg Crowns: Three of these territories were ruled by the House of Habsburg, while one remained a fiercely Lutheran northern rival!
clues.ahaFactoid: Under Gustavus Adolphus, Protestant Sweden famously smashed Habsburg imperial armies during the Thirty Years' War!

clues.stem: 47 BCE Victory Dispatch: Reporting a lightning five-day campaign in Pontus, Julius Caesar wrote to Rome: "I came, I saw, I [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: In crisp three-word Latin—"Veni, vidi, vici"—Caesar summed up the Battle of Zela for a triumph banner!

clues.stem: 1775 Virginia Firebrand: Urging colonial militias to arm against King George III, Patrick Henry thundered, "Give me liberty, or give me [ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Delivered inside St. John's Church in Richmond with George Washington and Thomas Jefferson listening in the pews!

clues.stem: July 4, 1776 Parchment: Thomas Jefferson opened the Declaration's sweeping promise: "We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Ben Franklin and John Adams lightly edited Jefferson's draft—changing "sacred and undeniable" to punchier "self-evident"!

clues.stem: Shakespeare's Senate Floor: Spotting his trusted friend holding a dagger on the Ides of March, Caesar whispers, "Et tu, [ _____ ]?"
clues.ahaFactoid: Ancient Roman historian Suetonius says Caesar actually spoke Greek in real life: "Kai su, teknon?" ("You too, my child?")!

clues.stem: Continental Humor: Signing the 1776 Declaration despite treason charges, Ben Franklin quipped, "We must all hang together, or most assuredly we shall all [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Franklin tossed that famous pun straight at John Hancock right after Hancock urged everyone to stay unanimous!

clues.stem: Succession Cry: Announcing zero gap in royal authority across centuries, heralds shout: "The King is dead, [ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: In 1422 France, "Le roi est mort, vive le roi!" ensured zero interregnum pause between monarchs!

clues.stem: 1775 Old North Steeple: Longfellow's midnight poem set Boston's secret signal for British troops marching out: "One if by land, and [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Sexton Robert Newman actually hung two lanterns in the church steeple for less than a minute before ducking Redcoat patrols!

clues.stem: Boston Rallying Cry: Protesting London's Stamp Act duties without colonial MPs in Parliament, patriots chanted, "No taxation without [ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Massachusetts lawyer James Otis helped ignite that slogan across town halls in the 1760s!

clues.stem: 1799 Eulogy: Saluting George Washington before Congress, Henry Lee penned the immortal tribute: "First in war, first in peace, and first in the [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: John Marshall actually read Lee's famous lines aloud inside a packed Philadelphia church because Lee wasn't present that day!

clues.stem: Luxor 1922 Candlelight: Peering through a tiny hole into Tutankhamun's untouched tomb, archaeologist Howard Carter gasped, "Yes, [ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Lord Carnarvon waited anxiously behind him in the dark tunnel and asked "Can you see anything?" right before Carter spoke those two words!

clues.stem: 1787 Preamble: Gouverneur Morris opened the U.S. Constitution with three towering words putting citizens above kings: "[ _____ ] of the United States."
clues.ahaFactoid: Earlier drafts listed every state individually by name until Gouverneur Morris condensed the preamble into three bold words!

clues.stem: Coronation Choir: Echoing through Westminster Abbey since 1745 whenever a male monarch reigns, Britain's national anthem sings "God Save the [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: After 70 years of "God Save the Queen," Britons flipped the lyrics back to "King" in September 2022 for Charles III!

clues.stem: 1415 Agincourt Rally: Outnumbered in muddy French fields, Shakespeare's King Henry V cheers his army as "we few, we happy few, we [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Stephen Ambrose later borrowed Henry V's stirring St. Crispin's Day line to title his classic WWII Easy Company chronicle!

clues.stem: Absolutist Legend: Though historians debate whether the young Sun King actually spoke it to parliament in 1655, legend quotes Louis XIV as saying "I am the [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: French "L'État, c'est moi" captured absolute monarchy so neatly that it stuck to Louis XIV—ironically, on his deathbed he sighed "I depart, but the state remains"!

clues.stem: Imperial Remodel: Boasting of his monuments across the Tiber, first Roman Emperor Augustus claimed, "I found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Opening Carrara quarries in northern Italy funded temples, baths, and Augustus's gleaming white Ara Pacis altar!

clues.stem: 1787 Exit Question: Asked outside Independence Hall whether Americans got a monarchy or a republic, Ben Franklin replied, "A republic, if you can [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Philadelphia socialite Elizabeth Willing Powel posed that famous question right as the Constitutional Convention wrapped up!

clues.stem: 1593 Pragmatism: Converting from Protestantism so France's war-weary capital would crown him king, Henry IV supposedly winked, "Paris is well worth a [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Five years later in 1598, that same Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes granting French Protestants rare religious tolerance!

clues.stem: 1485 Bosworth Field: unhorsed in Shakespeare's dramatic finale, doomed King Richard III screams out, "A horse! A horse! My [ _____ ] for a horse!"
clues.ahaFactoid: In reality, Richard III charged straight at Henry Tudor's banner and died fighting—ending the Wars of the Roses under a Leicester car park!

clues.stem: Chiseled on Arches & Manhole Covers: Rome's famous four-letter civic emblem S.P.Q.R. stands for "The Senate and the [ _____ ] of Rome."
clues.ahaFactoid: Modern Rome's city government STILL stamps "Senatus Populusque Romanus" on streetlamps, buses, and bronze plaques today!

clues.stem: Order of the Garter Motto: After Edward III retrieved a fallen garter at a ball, Britain's top knighthood adopted "Shame to him who [ _____ ] of it."
clues.ahaFactoid: Written in medieval Anglo-Norman French—"Honi soit qui mal y pense"—it still encircles the British royal coat of arms!

clues.stem: Broken Colossus Pedestal: Shelley's poem about fallen Pharaoh Ramesses II taunts rulers with the boast: "Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and [ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Inspired by a colossal granite statue of Ramesses II hauled to London's British Museum in 1817, the boast sat surrounded by empty sand!

clues.stem: 138 CE Imperial Farewell: Dying Roman Emperor Hadrian composed a gentle five-line Latin poem addressing his own wandering, charming little [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: "Animula vagula blandula" ("Little soul, wandering, charming") captured the cultured architect-emperor's final quiet humility!

clues.stem: I crossed the icy Delaware on Christmas night 1776, chaired the 1787 Convention, and retired twice back to my Virginia Mount Vernon farm. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hearing Washington planned to surrender his general's sword back to Congress in 1783, amazed King George III called him "the greatest character of the age"!

clues.stem: I organized Boston's Sons of Liberty, helped spark the 1773 Tea Party, signed the Declaration, and lent my name to a famous craft brewery. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Second cousin to President John Adams, Boston firebrand Samuel Adams worked for years as a modest maltster—not a commercial brewer!

clues.stem: Around the year 1000 CE—nearly five centuries before Columbus—my Norse crew sailed past Greenland to build sod huts in Newfoundland's "Vinland." Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Excavated at L'Anse aux Meadows in 1960, iron rivets and a bronze Norse cloak pin proved Leif's crew truly reached North America!

clues.stem: I designed my hilltop brick Monticello estate, doubled America with the Louisiana Purchase, and founded the University of Virginia. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Jefferson left out his two terms as U.S. President from his own tombstone epitaph—listing only Declaration author, Virginia religious freedom, and UVA!

clues.stem: I tied Thomas Jefferson in the chaotic 1800 electoral vote, served as 3rd U.S. Vice President, and dueled Alexander Hamilton at Weehawken. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: That deadlocked 1800 election prompted the 12th Amendment so presidents and vice presidents would never run on the same ballot tally again!

clues.stem: Folded over glowing charcoal by Japanese masters into a razor-sharp curved single edge, I formed the proud "soul" of every samurai. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Samurai wore the long katana paired with a shorter wakizashi tucked together in their sash—a matched duo called daisho!

clues.stem: Thrust onto the British throne after my brother Edward VIII abdicated in 1936, I worked past a childhood stammer to rally Britain during WWII. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Assisted by Australian speech therapist Lionel Logue, George VI's moving 1939 radio broadcast inspired Oscar winner The King's Speech!

clues.stem: President of the 1776 Continental Congress, I signed my name so huge across the parchment that my name now means any autograph! Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: As Congress's presiding officer, wealthy Boston merchant Hancock signed first in the dead center—leaving plenty of open ink space!

clues.stem: Built from overlapping oak planks with twin carved dragon prows, my shallow hull glided across stormy Atlantic waves AND narrow rivers. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Drawing barely three feet of water, a longship could run straight up onto sandy beaches so warriors leaped ashore dry-shod!

clues.stem: After waiting longer as heir apparent than anyone in British history, I ascended the throne in 2022 at age 73. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Born in 1948, Charles served as Prince of Wales for 64 years—eclipsing Edward VII's long wait as Victoria's heir!

clues.stem: Sailing across the English Channel from Normandy in 1066, I defeated Harold Godwinson at Hastings and changed English forever. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Every time an English speaker orders "beef" or "pork" instead of "cow" or "pig," they're speaking French imported by William's Norman barons!

clues.stem: Funded by Lord Carnarvon, I spent six dusty seasons digging in the Valley of the Kings before uncovering King Tut's golden stairs in 1922. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Started as a teenage archaeological watercolor artist in Egypt, Carter cataloged all 5,398 artifacts in Tut's tomb over ten meticulous years!

clues.stem: Famous for dueling Saladin in the Third Crusade, I spoke French fluently, spent bare months in England, and died from a crossbow bolt in 1199. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Though a statue of Richard I stands proud outside Westminster, he reportedly joked he'd sell London if only he could find a buyer!

clues.stem: Augustus's lifelong right-hand admiral, I won the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE and built the original temple where Rome's Pantheon stands! Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: When Emperor Hadrian rebuilt Rome's domed Pantheon a century later, he kept the original bronze dedication: "M. AGRIPPA FECIT"!

clues.stem: Standing barely 5-foot-4, I took detailed shorthand notes all summer in 1787, co-wrote The Federalist, and became the 4th U.S. President. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Quiet, bookish James Madison brought hundreds of political history books to Philadelphia—earning his nickname "Father of the Constitution"!

clues.stem: Undefeated in over 60 duels—even carving a wooden sword from a boat oar for Ganryu Island—I wrote The Book of Five Rings. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: In retirement inside a Kumamoto cave, swordmaster Musashi also painted sumi-e ink hawks and taught two-sword fighting!

clues.stem: Hiding in Somerset marshes before rallying Wessex against Viking armies, I built fortified burhs and am the ONLY English king called "the Great." Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: A scholar-king who translated Latin books into Old English, Alfred also invented candle-clocks notched to measure hours!

clues.stem: Fifth Mughal emperor of India, I commissioned the glittering Peacock Throne in Delhi and white-marble Taj Mahal for beloved Mumtaz Mahal. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Deposed by his own son Aurangzeb in 1658, Shah Jahan spent his final eight years gazing at the Taj Mahal from a palace balcony!

clues.stem: After besieging Paris in 911 CE, French king Charles the Simple bought me off with coastal land—making me the first Viking ruler of Normandy. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Five generations later, Rollo's great-great-great-grandson William the Conqueror sailed from Normandy to take England!

clues.stem: Replacing long throwing spears with short stabbing iklwa blades and "bull horn" flanking tactics, I forged a mighty kingdom in southern Africa. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Shaka drilled barefoot regiments able to march 50 miles a day across rugged Natal hills in the 1810s and 1820s!

clues.stem: Born a sandal-bearer of peasant stock, I avenged Oda Nobunaga, banned peasant swords in the 1588 Sword Hunt, and built Osaka Castle. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because he lacked noble Minamoto ancestry to claim "shogun," Hideyoshi ruled Japan as imperial regent (Kampaku and Taiko)!

clues.stem: One of Alexander's childhood friends and bodyguards, I claimed Egypt after his death, stole his golden funeral carriage, and founded the Library of Alexandria. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hijacking Alexander's mummy en route to Macedon gave Ptolemy I unmatched royal legitimacy—launching a 275-year Greek-Egyptian dynasty!

clues.stem: Before or After in Ancient Egypt: Which legendary ruler lived and ruled EARLIER in history?
clues.ahaFactoid: Boy King Tutankhamun died around 1323 BCE—more than 1,250 years before Cleopatra VII took Egypt's throne!

clues.stem: Before or After Across the Atlantic: Which voyage reached North America FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Norse sailors built timber-and-turf halls in Newfoundland around 1000 CE—nearly 500 years ahead of 1492!

clues.stem: Before or After in Revolutions: Which watershed political event happened FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: America declared independence in July 1776—thirteen years before Parisians stormed the Bastille on July 14, 1789!

clues.stem: Before or After in English History: Which royal milestone occurred FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Barons forced King John to seal Magna Carta in 1215—nearly three centuries before Henry VIII took the Tudor throne in 1509!

clues.stem: Before or After in Rome: Which Roman milestone happened FIRST—Caesar crossing the Rubicon or Mount Vesuvius burying Pompeii?
clues.ahaFactoid: Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE—128 years before Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE!

clues.stem: Before or After in Archaeology: Which Egyptian discovery came FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: French soldiers unearthed the Rosetta Stone in 1799 (deciphered in 1822)—a full century before Carter opened Tut's tomb in 1922!

clues.stem: Before or After in British Queens: Which English/British queen ascended the throne FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Mary I took the crown in 1553—five years ahead of half-sister Elizabeth I (1558), Anne (1702), and Victoria (1837)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Early America: Which presidential milestone happened FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: George Washington took the first oath in New York City in 1789—he was the ONLY U.S. President never to live inside the White House!

clues.stem: Before or After in Stone Monuments: Which iconic royal structure was built FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Giza's Great Pyramid (~2560 BCE) stood over 2,000 years before Athens built the Parthenon (438 BCE)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Samurai History: Which major 1860s turning point happened FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863—five years before Japan's 1868 Meiji Restoration ended shogun rule!

clues.stem: Before or After in World Empires: Which conqueror unified his realm FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Alexander carved his empire in the 330s-320s BCE—more than a century before Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BCE!

clues.stem: Before or After in Roman History: Which event happened EARLIER?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cleopatra died in 30 BCE—more than a century before Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE!

clues.stem: Before or After in Royal Wonders: Which royal landmark was constructed FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Emperor Yongle's Forbidden City opened in 1420—about 30 years before Pachacuti built Machu Picchu (~1450) and 230 years before Taj Mahal (1648)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Medieval Europe: Which event came FIRST—the Lindisfarne Viking raid or Charlemagne's imperial coronation?
clues.ahaFactoid: Norse raiders shocked Northumbria at Lindisfarne in 793—seven years before Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne on Christmas Day 800!

clues.stem: Before or After in Chronology: Which existed FIRST—Oxford University teaching scholars or the Aztec Empire founding Tenochtitlan?
clues.ahaFactoid: Oxford University was already teaching scholars for over two centuries before Mexica wanderers spotted the eagle on a cactus in 1325!

clues.stem: Before or After in 1400s Turning Points: Which dramatic event came FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453—32 years before Bosworth Field (1485) and 39 years before Columbus (1492)!

clues.stem: Before or After in Early 1600s History: Which milestone happened FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ieyasu crushed his rivals at foggy Sekigahara in 1600—seven years before English settlers landed at Jamestown, Virginia in 1607!

clues.stem: Before or After in Fallen Crowns: Which 20th-century monarchy collapsed FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Child Emperor Puyi abdicated in February 1912, ending 2,100 years of Chinese imperial dynasties five years before Tsar Nicholas II fell!

clues.stem: Before or After in Classical Antiquity: Which Persian milestone occurred FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cyrus the Great entered Babylon peacefully in 539 BCE—nearly half a century before Athens beat Darius I at Marathon in 490 BCE!

clues.stem: Before or After on the Silk Road: Which golden empire was founded FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Chang'an's cosmopolitan Tang court opened in 618 CE—over 130 years before Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur laid out Baghdad's Round City!

clues.stem: Before or After in Egypt's 18th Dynasty: Who expelled the Hyksos and wore Egypt's double crown FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Warrior pharaoh Ahmose I founded Egypt's glittering 18th Dynasty around 1550 BCE—generations before Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, or Tutankhamun!

clues.stem: Before or After in European Treaties: Which landmark religious settlement was signed FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Charles V signed the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 ("Whose realm, his religion")—43 years before Nantes (1598) and 93 before Westphalia (1648)!

clues.stem: According to Roman chroniclers, Egypt's last pharaoh Cleopatra VII chose to end her life in 30 BCE using the venom of what desert creature?
clues.ahaFactoid: Modern historians note a cobra wouldn't easily hide inside a basket of figs—leaving scholars wondering if she drank a fast poison elixir instead!

clues.stem: Weighing 24 pounds of solid gold inlaid with turquoise and blue lapis lazuli, Tutankhamun's funerary mask features what royal chin ornament?
clues.ahaFactoid: Egyptians strapped braided stone or gold beards onto pharaohs—even female ruler Hatshepsut—as a sacred sign of divine kingship!

clues.stem: Reforming Rome's chaotic lunar calendar into a neat 365.25-day solar year in 46 BCE, which dictator got the summer month Quintilis renamed after him?
clues.ahaFactoid: Before Julius Caesar added 90 extra days to 46 BCE ("The Last Year of Confusion"), Roman winter festivals drifted right into springtime!

clues.stem: Meaning "The Way of the Warrior," what unwritten Japanese moral code demanded fearlessness, frugality, and fierce loyalty from Samurai?
clues.ahaFactoid: A samurai left without a feudal lord to serve became a wandering "ronin"—literally translating to "wave man" drifting adrift on the sea!

clues.stem: To shed their German-sounding family surname "Saxe-Coburg and Gotha" during WWI in 1917, British royals adopted what castle's name?
clues.ahaFactoid: King George V picked "Windsor" after a clever courtier reminded him how ancient and quintessentially English Windsor Castle sounded!

clues.stem: Writing to her husband John at the 1776 Continental Congress, which sharp-minded future First Lady urged founders to "Remember the Ladies"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Abigail ran the family farm, traded bonds, and raised a future President (John Quincy Adams) while John spent years abroad in Europe!

clues.stem: Exiled from Iceland for manslaughter around 982 CE, which Viking named an icy giant "Greenland" purely as a clever real-estate sales pitch?
clues.ahaFactoid: Medieval sagas openly admit Erik picked a sunny green name betting folks would sail there eagerly if the land sounded fertile!

clues.stem: Right before dying in 1216, which famously unpopular Magna Carta monarch lost his baggage train—and England's Crown Jewels—in rising tidal mud?
clues.ahaFactoid: Crossing The Wash estuary at the wrong tide swallowed wagons of gold goblets, relics, and cash—never found by treasure hunters since!

clues.stem: When Pope Clement VII refused to annul his 24-year marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Henry VIII broke from Rome in 1534 to wed whom?
clues.ahaFactoid: Anne Boleyn lasted just three years as queen—yet their daughter grew up to become powerhouse Queen Elizabeth I!

clues.stem: Stretching 1,677 miles from Susa to Sardis with 111 fresh horse relay stations, which Persian king's Royal Road carried mail in seven days flat?
clues.ahaFactoid: Greek historian Herodotus praised Darius's couriers with the famous line carved on New York's Post Office: "Neither snow nor rain nor heat!"

clues.stem: Moving Rome's imperial capital east to Greek town Byzantium in 330 CE, which emperor renamed the Golden Horn metropolis after himself?
clues.ahaFactoid: For over 1,100 years, Constantinople guarded the Bosphorus with triple stone walls and a massive bronze harbor chain!

clues.stem: Hosting Hernan Cortes atop floating lake-garden causeways in 1519, who was the reigning Aztec emperor of Tenochtitlan?
clues.ahaFactoid: At Moctezuma's imperial zoo in Tenochtitlan, hundreds of keepers tended jaguars, eagles, and aviaries larger than any palace in 1519 Europe!

clues.stem: Rome Senate Wire, 44 BCE: Ignoring soothsayer Spurinna's famous warning to "Beware the [ _____ ]," Julius Caesar walked unarmed into Pompey's Theater.
clues.ahaFactoid: In the Roman calendar, the "Ides" simply marked the middle of the month (March 15)—when debts were due and the full moon shone!

clues.stem: Continental Army Wire, 1777: Leaving bloody footprints in the Pennsylvania snow, Washington's tattered army drilled into shape under Baron von Steuben at [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Remarkably, zero battles were fought at Valley Forge—it was a six-month winter endurance camp that forged amateurs into disciplined regulars!

clues.stem: London Telegraph: Steering Britain through steamships, railways, and global trade from 1837 to 1901, the [ _____ ] Era took its name from a long-reigning queen.
clues.ahaFactoid: Victoria ruled from age 18 until 81, witnessing photography, telegraphs, steam trains, and electric light transform London!

clues.stem: Virginia Wire, Oct 1781: Trapped between Washington's Continentals and French ships in Chesapeake Bay, Lord Cornwallis surrendered at [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Legend says British bands played a mournful tune called "The World Turned Upside Down" as redcoats marched out to stack muskets!

clues.stem: Norse Saga Dispatch: Warriors slain bravely with weapon in hand expected Valkyries to escort them to Odin's golden-shielded feast hall, [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: According to the Eddas, Valhalla boasted 540 colossal doors—each wide enough for 800 warriors to march out side by side at Ragnarok!

clues.stem: Ptolemaic Wire: Born in Mediterranean splendor beside the Pharos Lighthouse and Great Library, Cleopatra VII ruled from her coastal capital, [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Founded in 331 BCE, coastal Alexandria felt far more Greek than inland Nile cities—sporting marble theaters, gyms, and paved avenues!

clues.stem: Shogunate Castle Decree: To keep regional samurai lords too busy and broke to rebel, Tokugawa shoguns forced daimyo to spend every other year living in [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: This "alternate attendance" policy forced lords to fund huge marching retinues—accidentally booming inns, restaurants, and highways across Japan!

clues.stem: 9th-Century England Wire: Turning the northern city of York into bustling trading hub Jorvik, Norse settlers carved out a realm called the [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Hundreds of everyday English words—from "sky," "window," and "egg" to "knife" and "they"—entered English through Danelaw neighbors!

clues.stem: Mediterranean Wire: Stretching roughly 200 years from Augustus's rise in 27 BCE to Marcus Aurelius's death in 180 CE, Rome's golden stability is called the [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Though frontiers still saw skirmishes, smooth Mediterranean trade let olive oil, glass, and Egyptian grain move safely for two centuries!

clues.stem: 1214 Bouvines Wire: Crushing King John's coalition near Flanders, French Capetian king [ _____ ] permanently doubled royal domains across Normandy and Anjou.
clues.ahaFactoid: Before Philip II, French kings signed documents as "King of the Franks"—after his conquests, he boldly styled himself "King of France"!

clues.stem: Inspect Giza's limestone colossus on the Monitor: pairing a pharaoh's royal headdress with a crouching beast's paws, what mythical body sits beneath the head?
clues.ahaFactoid: Carved out of a single huge limestone ridge around 2500 BCE under Khafre, the Great Sphinx spent centuries buried up to its shoulders in Sahara sand!

clues.stem: Zoom in on Philadelphia's bronze Liberty Bell: cast with Leviticus's "Proclaim Liberty" verse, what famous jagged flaw silenced its clapper in 1846?
clues.ahaFactoid: The 2,080-pound bell cracked on its very first test ring in 1752—gets recast twice—and split wide open ringing for Washington's Birthday in 1846!

clues.stem: Sparkling inside London's Jewel House, Britain's Imperial State Crown weighs 2.3 pounds and houses the 317-carat Cullinan II what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cut from the largest rough diamond ever unearthed in 1905 South Africa, Cullinan II glitters right above the Velvet cap!

clues.stem: Look at an Edo samurai warrior's lacquered armor on the Monitor: sweeping golden horns or crescent moons sprout proudly from his helmet, called what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Commanders stuck outrageous giant crescents, seashells, or antlers onto their kabuto helmets so soldiers could spot their leader through battle smoke!

clues.stem: Spot the neat looped rope oval framing Egyptian hieroglyphs on temple walls: archaeologists call this royal nameplate ring a what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Napoleon's French soldiers thought the oval looked like a paper rifle cartridge—naming it "cartouche"—which later gave Champollion the key to decode hieroglyphs!

clues.stem: Look at this hammered solid-gold funerary mask dug from a Mycenaean royal shaft grave in 1876 by Heinrich Schliemann: which Greek king's name did it get?
clues.ahaFactoid: Later radiocarbon checks revealed the gleaming gold mask actually predates the Trojan War era by roughly 300 years (around 1550 BCE)!

clues.stem: Look at pharaohs wearing a tall white bowling-pin cone nested inside a curled red wicker basket: combining both hats formed the Pschent, symbolizing what?
clues.ahaFactoid: White Hedjet (southern Upper Egypt) plus red Deshret (northern Lower Delta) proclaimed one pharaoh ruled the entire Nile!

clues.stem: Zoom in on the wireless Bluetooth logo on phones: its crisp blue geometric symbol fuses two Viking Elder Futhark runes spelling whose initials?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ericsson engineer Jim Kardach combined Norse runes Hagall (H) and Bjarkan (B) for King Harald Bluetooth, who united warring tribes!

clues.stem: Peek beneath the wooden seat of England's 700-year-old oak Coronation Chair: a hollow shelf holds a 335-pound sandstone block from which kingdom?
clues.ahaFactoid: King Edward I hauled the Stone of Destiny south in 1296; returned to Edinburgh in 1996, it traveled back to London for Charles III's 2023 coronation!

clues.stem: Carved 300 feet high on an Iranian cliffside, Persian King Darius I's trilingual relief served as the Rosetta Stone for cuneiform. Name this cliff monument!
clues.ahaFactoid: British officer Henry Rawlinson dangled from ropes in the 1830s-1840s to copy Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian cuneiform off the sheer rock!

clues.stem: Longship Klaxon! Three of these Viking facts come straight from archaeology, while one Wagner-opera costume myth fools moviegoers!
clues.ahaFactoid: Zero horned Viking war helmets have ever been dug up—19th-century Swedish painters and Wagner's Ring opera costume designer invented them!

clues.stem: Tomb Klaxon! Three of these King Tut facts check out, while one sensational 1923 newspaper rumor turns Howard Carter's longevity upside down!
clues.ahaFactoid: Statistical check: out of 58 people present when Tut's tomb and sarcophagus opened, average lifespan matched normal peers—Carter lived 17 more years!

clues.stem: 1775 Midnight Klaxon! Three of these Paul Revere facts are true, while one shouted slogan would have blown his secret cover right past Redcoat patrols!
clues.ahaFactoid: Colonists still considered themselves British in April 1775—Revere quietly whispered at doors that "the Regulars are coming out"!

clues.stem: Founders Klaxon! Three of these George Washington tales are rock-solid history, while one boyhood honesty parable was cooked up by a biographer!
choices: He ran a Mount Vernon whiskey still
He refused a royal king title
clues.ahaFactoid: Traveling bookseller Parson Mason Weems invented the cherry-tree confession in 1806—seven years after Washington died—to sell biographies!

clues.stem: Alexandria Klaxon! Three of these Cleopatra VII facts are 100% genuine, while one claim gets her Macedonian Greek family tree completely backwards!
clues.ahaFactoid: Cleopatra belonged to the Greek-Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty founded by Alexander's general—born 2,500 years after Pyramid builder Khufu!

clues.stem: Roman Klaxon! Three of these Julius Caesar facts are true history, while one restaurant rumor mixes up a dictator with a 1924 Tijuana chef!
clues.ahaFactoid: Italian immigrant restaurateur Caesar Cardini tossed the famous romaine-and-parmesan salad in Tijuana, Mexico on July 4, 1924!

clues.stem: 1776 Klaxon! Three of these Declaration of Independence facts are accurate, while one famous painting illusion gets the signing calendar wrong!
choices: King George got news in August
clues.ahaFactoid: Congress approved the wording on July 4, yet most delegates actually lined up to sign the big engrossed parchment on August 2, 1776!

clues.stem: Sengoku Klaxon! Three of these samurai warfare facts check out, while one romantic movie trope ignores how enthusiastically warlords adopted firearms!
clues.ahaFactoid: After Portuguese matchlocks landed at Tanegashima in 1543, Japanese smiths produced more guns per capita than almost any nation in Europe!

clues.stem: Hellenistic Klaxon! Three of these Alexander tales appear in ancient sources, while one misquotes Plutarch on why the king actually cried over infinite universes!
choices: His horse Bucephalus got a city
He wept having zero worlds left
clues.ahaFactoid: Plutarch wrote Alexander wept hearing philosopher Anaxarchus say infinite worlds exist—lamenting he hadn't even conquered ONE completely yet!

clues.stem: Antiquity Klaxon! Three of these Roman palace/arena facts are true, while one notorious Latin translation error invents a disgusting banquet room!
clues.ahaFactoid: From Latin "vomere" (to spew forth), a "vomitorium" was simply a wide vaulted stadium walkway designed to empty 50,000 spectators fast!

clues.stem: 50/50 Roman Title: Was Julius Caesar legally Rome's first official Emperor, or a Republic Dictator?
clues.ahaFactoid: Caesar refused a royal crown at Lupercalia as "Dictator Perpetuo"—leaving Augustus (27 BCE) as Rome's true first Emperor!

clues.stem: 50/50 Stars & Stripes: Did Philadelphia seamstress Betsy Ross create the 5-pointed star legend in family lore, or sign the Declaration of Independence?
clues.ahaFactoid: Betsy Ross's grandson William Canby went public with the five-point star story in 1870—nearly a century after 1776!

clues.stem: 50/50 Viking Funerals: Did elite Scandinavian Vikings usually bury chieftains inside earth mounds on land, or shoot flaming arrows at drifting ships?
clues.ahaFactoid: Dramatic flaming arrow boats are pure Hollywood—real finds like Norway's 1904 Oseberg ship were preserved inside clay burial mounds!

clues.stem: 50/50 Nile Timeline: Were the Great Pyramids of Giza already ancient ruins to Cleopatra VII, or built by her Ptolemaic architects?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cleopatra walked past pyramids that were already older to her than ancient Rome is to smartphone users today!

clues.stem: 50/50 Presidential Date: Did George Washington pass away at Mount Vernon in the 1790s or survive into the 1800s?
clues.ahaFactoid: Catching severe throat infection after riding across his snowy farms, Washington died on December 14, 1799—just weeks shy of 1800!

clues.stem: 50/50 Founding Coincidence: Did rivals-turned-friends John Adams and Thomas Jefferson die on the exact same date—July 4, 1826?
clues.ahaFactoid: On the exact 50th anniversary of the Declaration, 90-year-old Adams murmured "Thomas Jefferson survives"—unaware Jefferson had died hours earlier!

clues.stem: 50/50 Crown Power: In what year did a British monarch LAST exercise Royal Assent veto power to block a bill passed by Parliament?
clues.ahaFactoid: No British monarch has refused Royal Assent since Queen Anne rejected the Scottish Militia Bill in March 1708!

clues.stem: 50/50 Imperial Wardrobe: Was Roman purple silk/wool dye pressed from Mediterranean sea snails or crushed desert lapis stone?
clues.ahaFactoid: Over 10,000 spiny sea snails yielded barely one gram of Tyrian purple—making imperial purple togas worth more per ounce than gold!
